#4522. Upward Mobility: 1997 $30K Luxury Sedans Compared

Nine ways—Acura 3.2TL, Cadillac Catera, Ford Taurus SHO, Infiniti I30, Lexus ES300, Mazda Millenia, Mitsubishi Diamante, Saab 900SE, Volvo 850GLT—to express yourself on the way to the top.

From the February 1997 issue of Car and Driver.

Let’s say your corporate star is rising. Your cozy cubicle has been swapped for an office with floor-to-ceiling walls and a door. Your annual salary just achieved that magic sixth digit. The paint is drying on your first personalized parking space. Now the question is, what are you going to park on that providential piece of pavement?

You’ve worked hard and earned the right to drive something special. You want to make a statement about who you are and where you’re headed, but you must choose wisely. From time to time, you’ll be the designated driver shuttling your foursome from the three-martini lunch to the links, so a sports car is out. Your spouse already drives a sport-utility vehicle, so a sedan it must be. It would be impolitic to outzoot the boss with a flashier car, so you’ll be shopping in the “near luxury” segment.

Prepare to spend more than the cost of the fanciest family cars that top out around $28,000 but don’t cross the luxury-tax threshold of $34,000. This way you’ll send the message that you’re a good ol' fiscal conservative, anti-tax type.

See all results for used cars for sale near 14094

Our Buyers Guide lists 17 sedans in that price range. We eliminated five of those based on prior com­parison-test standings and road-test results. We excluded the BMW 3-series and the Mercedes C-class because reason­ably equipped models only evade the luxury tax in four-cylinder guise and their subcompact interior dimensions make them less suitable transportation for four corporate execs. That last argument also ruled out the lovely Audi A4. The remaining nine cars are the cream of this crop. Each should easily satisfy the middle man­ager’s needs and caprices.

Since we last evaluated this class in August 1994, the Acura TL, the Cadillac Catera, and the Infiniti I30 have joined the seg­ment. The Ford Taurus SHO sprouted a V-8, lost its manual trans­mission, and was recast as—in Ford’s words—an “executive express.” The Lexus ES300 and the Mitsubishi Diamante have been redesigned, the Volvo 850GLT has been given a new light-pressure turbocharged engine, and the Saab 900SE V-6 was promoted into our price range. The Mazda Millenia S, with its supercharged Miller-cycle engine, has drifted up in price, so we invited the normally aspirated L model instead.

The field includes seven 24-valve V-6 engines, one turbocharged five-­cylinder, and a 32-valve V-8. Each spins through a four-speed automatic trans­mission (only Infiniti offers a stick). There are two Swedes, one true Yank, one German/Yank (the Opel-derived Cadillac), and five Japanese in the bunch. Each speaks with a slightly different accent of luxury, style, and class.

In straight-line acceleration, the pack ­is remarkably tight—seven of the nine cars perform within 0.3 second of the average 0-to-60-mph and quarter-mile times. Handling behavior varies more widely, as does each manufacturer’s interpretation of luxury equipment.

See all results for used cars for sale near 14094

Although none of these cars is spartan, none is fully loaded, either. For example, not one car in this group is equipped with all four of these less-than-exotic items: traction control, a CD player, remote key­less entry, and variable intermittent wipers. Only three have heated seats. Just two have dual-zone climate controls. The Saab alone has a trip computer.

To fully appreciate the subtle person­ality traits of these nine middle-manage­ment-grade luxo-cruisers, we headed for the Hocking Hills of southeast Ohio. Here's how the cars stacked up.

For those climbing the corporate ladder at an avant-garde corporation, the Saab 900SE is a must-have. It fairly screams “I’m different and proud of it” to parking­ lot passersby. From its quirky ignition switch on the floor to its unmistakable shape to its tall-dining-room-chair front seats, this is the car with its baseball cap on backward.

Some of the 900’s quirks are quite useful, like the rear hatch and the split-folding back seat (with armrest pass­through) that, when folded, allows this car to swallow more than 50 cubic feet of cargo or a box measuring, in inches, 62 by 34 by 25. Other quirks are less endearing, like the upright, far-away, 747-style wind­shield that limits the view of overhead traffic lights.

The 900SE also has one of the smallest and least comfortable rear seats. Its low cushion provides Viking-scale headroom at the expense of thigh support and legroom. On the upside, there are three shoulder belts in back, each of which has a lever on the latch that allows the lap belt to be cinched tight for child­-seat installation or for restraining riders during exu­berant driving.

Our Saab cast the smallest shadow of any car in this group, and it racked up the highest skidpad grip (0.81 g, tied with the Mazda) and the best braking performance (168 feet from 70 mph). But a lack of road feel through the steering and considerable understeer conspired with the 2.5-liter V-6’s lack of low-end grunt to limit the Saab’s ability to generate grins out in the twisties.

The 900SE comes equipped with crea­ture comforts like heated power seats with three-position memory, rear-seat air vents, an eight-function trip computer, and a sporting traction-control system that doesn’t slow the car down as much as other systems do. But the interior looks plasticky, and noise levels are the highest of the bunch. Its jiggly, coarse ride ranks just above that of the roughrider Taurus.

HIGHS: High-capacity hatchback design, superb brakes, bags of character.LOWS: Lack of low-end punch, cramped back seat.VERDICT: The round peg in a square-hole segment.

Saab’s near-luxury formula is harder edged and less refined than its competitors’. We think that approach better suits those 900 models priced in the twenties.

From the backward baseball cap, we turn to the navy pinstripe suit. The Acura 3.2TL is the corporate yes man of this bunch. From its anonymous but handsome exterior to its mid­pack-performing engine and chassis to its well-appointed, conservative interior, this car meets, but never exceeds, the minimal requirements spelled out in its job description.

The TL drew its loudest praise during the highway slog down to southern Ohio. Editors lauded its low-cowl visibility, its smooth ride on the freeway, its rich-looking gath­ered leather and reasonably convincing fake-wood interior trim, and its impeccable Japanese build quality. There was some grumbling about the coarseness of its aging 3.2-liter V-6 and the transmission’s tendency to hunt for gears and select them sharply, but there was unanimous praise for the slalom­-gate shifter.

Unfortunately, that Germanic shifter suggests a sporting demeanor that the rest of the car doesn’t support. For starters, it seemed impossible to get completely comfortable in the driver’s seat because there is no place to rest one’s left foot. The plastic dead pedal is positioned more than four inches far­ther away than the accelerator, which puts it out of reach. The steering feels numb on center and then turns in sharply without delivering much road feel. The tires offer just 0.76 g of grip, the lowest of the group (tied with the Lexus). The TL’s smooth ride is offset by a lack of rebound control when the going gets rough. “Wow, I start driving like a little old lady in this car,” said one ordinarily enthusiastic driver.

Super-slab cruising is the TL’s forte, but it’s not the class leader in that category, either. Rear-seat com­fort is compromised by a low cushion and uncomfortable armrests. Engine noise is on the high end of the range in this class, and the 14- cubic-foot trunk is narrow in back with many intrusions to pack around.

HIGHS: Smooth, syrupy freeway ride; gated shifter; rich interior appointments.LOWS Legs-akimbo driving position, coarse engine, underdamped chassis. VERDICT: The Waylon Smithers of the group—eager to please, unable to excite.

We prefer cars that show a bit more initiative. Acura’s agreeable, play-it-safe TL sends the wrong message from our parking space.

This burly brute in its athletic­-cut Armani seems just a bit out of place in this group—as if its rise to power may have involved a little rough stuff. The Taurus SHO is the longest and widest car here, and it’s motivated by the only V-8 engine.

That engine is largely respon­sible for transforming the pure­bred, hard-nosed sport-sedan SHO of old into today’s gentrified “executive express.” Trouble is, that transformation is not com­plete. The smooth and sonorous V-8, although less potent than the old V-6, is quite competitive in this class. It’s the interior and chassis that need a promotion to executive grade.

Five fit comfortably on-board, but the stark monochrome inte­rior offers no suggestions that the car is at all special. The texture of the plastic dash-and-door trim resembles, well, plastic. New leather bucket seats provide good lateral support, especially at shoulder level, but they look inexpensive.

The chassis tuning is classic American sporty—lots of roll con­trol with rock-hard bushings that telegraph small-bump harshness, and softened springs to swallow the big stuff. “I didn’t know the road was so bumpy until I drove this car,” wrote one of us, who later lamented a Rice Krispies-like chorus of interior squeaks and creaks elicited by the harsh ride. Sadly, that harshness doesn’t pay off in superla­tive handling. Although it corners flatly with 0.80 g of grip, the SHO’s large size makes it a bit unwieldy on winding roads and in our emergency lane-change maneuver.

The engine, despite its eager note, is peaky by nature. There’s too little torque on tap at low revs, and overly tall gearing makes it slow to rev. In almost every acceleration test, the five-cylinder Volvo 850GLT trounced the SHO. And yet, predictably, the SHO’s fuel economy on this trip—18 mpg—was the group’s worst.

HIGHS: Unmistakable V-8 burble, big interior, lots of car for the money.LOWS: Low-buck interior, peaky engine, punishing ride.VERDICT: A ruffian among Rhode scholars.

The SHO sports the most fiscally pru­dent price in the group ($30,585), but it needs a Dale Carnegie course to round out its personality before it earns true “exec express” status.

Just beneath the chrome façade of this luxo-cruiser lies the honest middle-class values of a two-time Ten Best-winning Nissan Maxima. We’ve always been fond of Nissan’s lively 3.0-liter V-6 and its crisp, responsive steering, so we expected the I30 to impress us in this comparison.

In the corporate climb from family car to near-luxo status symbol, the Maxima gains a number of standard power acces­sories, a terrific Bose audio system with CD player, a softened suspension, and styling upgrades inside and out.

Parked alongside its competitors, the I30’s exterior looks gussied up and lacks the cohesive and clean beauty of the ES300 and the Diamante. The interior upgrades are more successful. Gathered leather on the seats and doors and respectable-looking faux-wood trim befit a car competing in this class. The seats are quite comfortable, although the rear seat­back is reclined a bit more than we like.

The V-6 achieves average acceleration and above-average fuel economy with the tallest gearing in this group. The softened suspension smooths out one-wheel bumps admirably, but when two wheels thwack an expansion joint at the same time, the seat and the steering wheel rever­berate, revealing this Infiniti’s humble family-car roots. Increased pitch, dive, and roll combine with howling tires to sap the fun out of twisty-road running (and they drop the I30 to last place in our lane-change test).

A $2200 Touring package buys trac­tion control, a limited-slip differential, bigger tires, and sport-suspension tuning. So equipped, an I30 might have fared better in this test, but none was available at test time.

HIGHS: Quiet, comfortable interior; low price.LOWS: Overly gussied-up exterior, weak-kneed suspension.VERDICT: A middle-of-­the-road middle-manager’s machine.

At $30,795, our I30 was equipped with heated seats, an integrated garage­-door opener, and remote-control one-­touch lowering of all four windows. But the I30’s jack-of-all-trades, master-of­-none demeanor makes a loaded Maxima SE look like the better buy. We wonder then, was the Maxima’s promotion to this class a textbook example of the Peter Prin­ciple at work?

Mazda’s Millenia has an “old money” patrician feel about it. Originally intended to spearhead Mazda’s aborted Amati line of high-end cars, its build quality, panel fits, and freedom from vibration, squeaks, and rattles are world-class. The body has a graceful and balanced look with a low, broad stance on the road. Such presence!

Inside, some editors carped about the almost military appearance of the dark-colored dash, but the material quality and the attention to detail are nonpareil. To wit: Carpeting lines the sides of the front seat cushions where leather might otherwise chafe against plastic to make noise. It’s well equipped, too, with traction control and heated seats and the group’s only infi­nitely adjustable electric tilting steering wheel. Of course, with a price that tiptoes into luxo-tax land at $34,049, it should be loaded. The rear seat, however, offers too little thigh support, no toe room, and uncomfortable armrests.

Ride and handling are bal­anced expertly. The Mil­lenia’s steering provides a strong sense of straight-ahead and excellent road feel. The chassis clings to the road with 0.81 g of grip, which ties with the Saab for top honors. Best of all, the ride quality doesn’t suffer—most road imperfections are heard more than they are felt.

So why is this limber aris­tocrat warming the fifth-place podium? Mainly because its 170-horse 2.5-liter engine is hopelessly outgunned here. “Definitely works overtime to make power, and it still comes up short,” said one tester. Its 9.2-second acceleration to 60 mph was almost a second slower than every other car, and its 6.1-second 50-to-70-mph passing time kept the Millenia trapped behind trucks on two-lane high­ways, while its driver waited impatiently for extra-wide passing gaps.

HIGHS: Build quality, chassis dynamics, Mazda rarity.LOWS: Overworked, underfed engine; uncomfortable rear-seat cushion.VERDICT: A charm-school graduate that needs to head for the gym.

Those who are smitten by the Mil­lenia’s chassis charms and its low-volume cachet might want to wait for another pro­motion and buy the $37,289 Miller-engined Millenia S (unless the boss already drives one).

Cadillac’s near-luxo nominee comes with a fresh green card and a thick German accent, although it’s gone shopping at Men’s Wearhouse for a Yankee wardrobe. We think it should have kept the Deutsche duds, but beneath the cluttered and cliched exterior lies a true autobahn stormer.

Editors filled the logbook with glow­ing praise about the Catera’s secure, stable, and well-weighted steering, its firm brakes, and the neutral handling demeanor of this group’s only rear-drive entrant. Classic Teutonic body rigidity helps this Cadillac absorb bumps with a single audible thunk and no reverberations. It has a Euro-firm but supple ride.

The Catera weighs in at 3794 pounds—the heaviest car here by 264 pounds—so it was not the quickest car on our handling loop. But its superb chassis control inspired a level of confidence that few of these cars could match.

A variable-resonance intake system broadens the 3.0-liter V-6’s torque curve substantially, so the Catera runs rings around the Mil­lenia (with which it shares a disad­vantageous weight-to-power ratio of 19 pounds per horsepower), despite having taller gearing.

Inside, the tall, chair-like seats—­front and back—drew praise for their lateral support and, again, Teutonic headroom. The Catera’s continental switchgear was viewed by many as subpar in refinement and ergonomic functionality, how­ever, and the European cigarette­-lighter socket is too large to fit American accessory plugs. Our Volvo has an Amer­ican lighter—why doesn’t the Cadillac?

The two-tone-gray dash is busy and button-encrusted, but then our $33,635 base Catera was adorned with more fea­tures and amenities than any of its com­petitors, including dual-zone climate con­trols with rear-seat vents, automatic headlamps, one-touch-down windows all around, and steering-wheel radio controls.

HIGHS: Stable, confident ride and handling on the autobahn as well as on our “Hockingheim” circuit.LOWS: Out-of-fashion exterior, excessive avoirdupois, low-grade Euro-switchgear.VERDICT A German athlete in need of a diet and a makeover.

The Catera is a strong contender in this class. Its eccentricities are mostly charming. To reach the head of this class, it needs to lose some weight and update its wardrobe.

This multinational player was con­ceived in Japan and born in Australia, but it speaks fluent Luxury with a perfect American accent. Check the stats: biggest interior with the most comfortable back seat, biggest-displacement engine making the most torque. Now check the ratings sheet: top marks in the ride and comfort—­and styling—categories.

The interior trim, in rich contrasting hues of butterscotch and mocha, also sug­gests an American heritage, especially the center console, which is slathered with too much fake wood. Still, the front and rear seats afford stretch-out room that only the Taurus can match, and the Diamante’s seat cushions are a model for the class. The armrests are all properly positioned and comfortable—it’s a little thing, but one that none of the others managed to get right. In back, there is ample room for toes knees, heads, and three sets of shoul­ders combined with a better view out than in the SHO. Throw in adjustable rear-seat headrests, front and rear reading lamps, and a comfortable shoulder belt for the center rear seat, and it’s easy to see why we deemed this the only true New York-to-L.A. back seat of the bunch.

Those who set out on such a journey will appreciate the Dia­mante’s class-leading interior quietness and its ride-tuned sus­pension, which fairly smothers all manner of road imperfections.

The driver will also appreciate the Diamante V-6’s 231 pound­-feet of torque, which propel this big boy off the line, out of tight corners, and around slower traffic quickly and without breathing hard.

But when the road turns twisty, get out the Dramamine. That smooth-riding suspension rolls over and plays dead when pushed. Howling understeer on the handling loop brought sweat to the brow of one editor, prompting this logbook entry: “It’s like the steering and the sus­pension haven’t been introduced.”

HIGHS: Pressed and creased styling; gorgeous, cavernous interior; torquey V-6.LOWS: Floats and corners like a traditional Yankee land yacht.VERDICT: The long-haul cruiser of this bunch.

The globe-trotting Diamante needs to spend some time studying road manners in Europe. For now, it’s a terrific luxo-cruiser on the American plan.

Meet the come-from-behind go-getter of the group. Volvo’s new light-pressure turbocharger transforms the 850 from a coarse, unrefined, and underpowered also-ran to the bullet-train of this class. Five cars can best its 190 horsepower, and six can out-twist its 191 pound-feet of torque, but a tiny turbo that spools up instantly provides max torque at a low, low 1800 rpm.

Mounted in a 3188-pound box, that translates to range-topping scoot: 0 to 60 mph in 7.0 seconds, the quarter-mile in 15.4 seconds at 91 mph, and passing times that are roughly a half-second ahead of the pack. And this acceleration arrives smoothly, without the neck-snapping boost of the full-blown Volvo turbos.

But this is no one-trick pony. It also squirts around twisty roads with elan. Its scrappy little Michelin MXV4s hang on with stoic silence right up to their 0.79-g limit, while the cloth seats grip the driver. The steering and the brakes are linear and communicative, and that mighty-mite motor champs at the bit at every apex.

Ride quality suffers little in the name of handling. The tires and the bushings absorb most sharp impacts, and the body structure—it exceeds the rigidity of any other 850 we’ve driven, although no struc­tural enhancements have been publi­cized for 1997—absorbs the big bumps with minimal fuss.

The passenger cube provides rea­sonable space and comfort for four or five occupants, each of whom gets a shoulder belt and a headrest, and there are side airbags in front. The rear seats fold independently, and the front pas­senger seat also folds forward for car­rying long objects. The interior is not as rich-looking as some, although leather seats ($1195) and a wood dash ($810) are options. Still, our $32,330 850GLT was equipped with most of what a mid­grade exec needs—except traction control, which adds $325.

HIGHS: Bullet-train performance and handling; safe, comfortable interior.LOWS: Even the exhaust pipe is square.VERDICT: The Norse god of executive transport, with a face only a Swede could love.

Two things kept this perfor­mance champ from grabbing the brass ring: Its Eighties cubist styling (“Goes like stink, with looks to match,” quipped one smart aleck) and past experience with far less robust 850s, which concerned us that this one might be a ringer.

You know the fair-haired, golden-boy Dudley Doright type at the office that everyone loves to hate? The ES300 is that guy. Cultured, athletic, suave, good­looking—the Lexus won top marks in eight of our 13 voting categories. We suspect the other cars were sneering at this one when no one was looking.

Every inch of the ES300 looks expensive, from its wind-chis­eled, two-tone exterior to its leather- and genuine-wood­-trimmed interior. Even the plastic panels look and feel like leather.

At $33,822, our test car lacked traction control, heated seats, and a CD player, but the entry-­level Lexus’s ability to do everything well so impressed us that it took top honors in the value category.

The ES300’s 200-horse 3.0-liter V-6 and four-speed automatic trans­mission established the class bench­mark for smoothness and delivered 60-mph, quarter-mile, and passing acceleration times within a couple tenths of the V-8-powered SHO’s.

In the chassis department, a new, cockpit-adjustable suspension al­lowed the ES300 to tie the Diamante’s top score in ride and match the Volvo’s winning scores in the handling and fun-to-drive categories. Set to “Sport,” the shocks help limit body roll and maintain optimal tire contact with the road in quick maneu­vers like our emergency lane change. The ES300 took a 4-mph lead over the Volvo in that test, despite wearing the least-grippy tires in the group.

Set to “Comfort,” the chassis absorbs large bumps and dips grace­fully, with a bit more float. Firmer bushings in the Lexus give the Dia­mante an advantage over small irreg­ularities, however.

A two-inch wheelbase stretch for 1997 has improved rear-seat comfort, especially with three passengers in back, by reducing wheelhouse intru­sion. But the new, slimmer sunroof design still compromises headroom somewhat.

HIGHS: Dream Whip drivetrain, Ritz-Carlton interior, Swiss-Army suspension.LOWS: Missing a few key features.VERDICT: An overachiever that does almost everything well.

Is the ES300 the perfect car in this segment? No. For that we’d need to hold the price and add the Cadillac’s features, the Diamante’s back seat, and the Volvo’s turbo. But its com­prehensive competence sends the message we’d want delivered from our personalized parking spot.

#4521. Pagani Reveals Final Huayra 70 One-Off With a Manual Gearbox

Mercedes Sales Plunge 31% in China as It Eyes Bigger US Push

Car Loan Fraud Is Costing Billions As AI Makes Scams Harder To Spot

New Toyota RAV4 Has A Comfort Issue Some Owners Can't Ignore

Pagani’s birthday bash just got its final guest, as the third special Huayra rolls out for everyone to see.

Mercedes Sales Plunge 31% in China as It Eyes Bigger US Push

Car Loan Fraud Is Costing Billions As AI Makes Scams Harder To Spot

New Toyota RAV4 Has A Comfort Issue Some Owners Can't Ignore

Used EVs Are Selling Faster Than Gas Cars, but Tesla Isn't Leading

Pagani has completed its Huayra 70 trilogy by revealing the Huayra 70 Anima. This unique car joins the other two special editions, marking the end of the founder’s 70th birthday celebration. For fans of manual transmissions, this model includes one as well.

The Huayra 70 series began with the Trionfo, built by Pagani’s Grandi Complicazioni team. Next up was the Huayra 70 Derecho, which showed off at Goodwood earlier this year. This one mixed Pearl Orange with deep Inky Blue for maximum visual drama. But the real headline was under the hood: an 864-horsepower twin-turbo V12 and a seven-speed manual.

Now, the trilogy is complete. Pagani just dropped the Huayra 70 Anima at the Wynn Las Vegas Concours, giving us one last, very different take on the Huayra formula. ‘Anima’ means soul in Italian, and this one definitely has its own vibe.

The Anima stands out with deep metallic blue paint, exposed carbon fiber, and just enough silver and light-blue accents to keep things interesting. It’s an open-top, with sculpted bodywork wrapping the cockpit and roll hoops that look ready for anything.

Up front, the Anima sports a low nose, gaping air intakes, and a splitter that means business. The sides show off wild aero, beefy rear haunches, and a rear wing that refuses to be ignored. Out back, there’s more exposed carbon, an angry diffuser, and a six-pipe exhaust setup that looks ready to wake the neighbors.

Inside, it’s a blue-and-white affair. White leather wraps the seats and most of the cockpit, with blue accents popping up everywhere. Exposed machined aluminum is scattered across the dash, steering wheel, and center console. As always, Pagani’s switchgear is a work of art – every piece looks like it belongs in a jewelry case.

The Anima keeps it old-school with three pedals and a manual shifter, complete with exposed linkage so you can watch the mechanical magic happen. The gear lever matches the blue-and-white theme, and a plaque reminds you this is number 3 of 3 – so don’t expect to see another one at Cars and Coffee.

Pagani’s keeping the Anima’s full specs under wraps for now, but it’s likely packing the same Mercedes-AMG 6.0-liter twin-turbo V12 as the Derecho. That means 864 hp, 811 pound-feet of torque, and all of it going to the rear wheels through a seven-speed manual. We’ll update when Pagani spills more details.

Like its siblings, the Huayra 70 Anima is a one-off, not something you’ll see at your local dealership. Pagani’s Grandi Complicazioni team handled the build, as usual for these ultra-bespoke projects.

No official price yet, but with all the custom work, rare materials, and one-of-one status, you can bet the sticker shock will be real. As for availability, this one’s spoken for, and with Anima rounding out the Huayra 70 trio, don’t expect any more to pop up with this badge.

#4520. BYD sold more EVs last month than the US did all quarter, topping 300,000

BYD sold over 300,000 electric vehicles in October, a new record and more than the US managed in the entire third quarter.

The world’s leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company’s highest monthly total in 2026.

BYD’s battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark.

To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates.

October marked BYD’s sixth straight month of higher sales growth and its third straight month of higher EV sales. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 electric vehicles, up 6% from the same period last year.

BYD’s all-electric vehicles (EVs) accounted for about 63% of total sales last month. Plug-in hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, fell 17% in October to 177,382 units. Through October, BYD’s PHEV sales fell 11% to 1,625,969 units.

According to BYD’s filing, the company exported 170,194 vehicles in October as it expands overseas to drive growth in markets like Europe, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America.

Through October, BYD exported over 1.5 million electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, nearly double compared to last year.

By the end of 2026, BYD expects overseas shipments to reach about 2 million vehicles. In 2027, that number is expected to rise to more than 2.5 million vehicles.

Market is in transition. BYD is dominant, but Geely and others have strong portfolios as well. Legacy manufacturers are slow walking, constrained by habit and unable to make critical strategic decisions in the face of the onslaught.

With several new and updated vehicles launching with its new Blade Battery 2.0 and Flash Charging technology, BYD aims to continue attracting new buyers with longer range, faster charging, and more tech-oriented models.

While the US is coming off its best quarter of the year in EV sales, BYD’s performance shows how far ahead China is in the transition to electric vehicles.

China continues to lead the global EV market, accounting for over half of all electric cars sold worldwide.

With a wave of low-cost domestic brands flooding China’s market, BYD and other automakers are driving growth overseas in major markets like Europe, South Korea, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America, where legacy OEMs are already falling behind quickly.

#4519. AI-Powered Coffee Runs And Service Visits Are Coming To Rivians In 2027

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Rivian's AI assistant will soon order coffee on your route so it’s fresh when you arrive at a coffee shop.

Future updates will automatically diagnose vehicle issues and book service appointments behind the scenes.

Rivian aims to eventually let owners control virtually every vehicle function through voice and AI.

When Rivian launched its in-house AI assistant in May, the company promised that the tech would soon do far more than answer ChatGPT-style questions, switch on the A/C, or text your friends. It pitched a chatbot that could be deeply integrated into your R1S or R2—but also deeply integrated into your life.

The Assistant hit the scene with Google Calendar capability, allowing drivers to move meetings on the fly, and Gmail came in October. In an interview on the Plugged-In Podcast this week, Rivian Chief Software Officer Wassym Bensaid said flashier integrations are coming soon, including one that will overhaul the service experience for Rivian owners.

"What I'm really excited about is the possibility in the future where you can bring your own personal digital ecosystem to the car through these AI integrations, and then also the possibility that you can start integrating with multiple other agentic experiences," he said.

One example: ordering coffee on your way to work. Bensaid said the Assistant will be able to help you order coffee from the right place at the right time, so that it's at the right temperature when you swing by.

The Rivian Assistant can answer general knowledge questions, control the vehicle, and integrate with a driver's Google Calendar and Gmail.

Thanks to AI, the experience of getting a Rivian serviced will become a lot smoother and more automated, he said. Rivian's AI tech will soon proactively diagnose issues, set up service appointments for owners, and make sure the service center has the right parts before an owner arrives, he said.

"That's a complete paradigm shift in that entire experience, and not only enables us to have a much more delightful experience for customers, but then it's a big efficiency lever for us and it helps us be much more competitive from a cost standpoint for something like service," he said.

We asked when exactly Rivian owners can expect these features to hit their vehicles. Bensaid said a lot of them are already in the works but need to get more reliable before a wider release.

"We're very close," he said. "We're talking about things that we will launch in 2027."

To check out our full Wassym Bensaid interview, head to Spotify, Apple, or scroll down to the video player below.

Rivian has an ambitious tech vision for its AI. And the Rivian Assistant is already impressive in some ways. But owners have also complained about shortcomings. I asked Bensaid about those growing pains.

"Similar to other features, other technologies, there's still tuning, and there's still some refinements that we need to continue doing," he said. "A lot of them is on us, which is great. Some of them are work with our partners in terms of how we ground some of the requests and how we really optimize them."

But getting today's features right is only part of the challenge. Rivian ultimately wants the Assistant to handle virtually anything drivers can do through the touchscreen.

"Our philosophy is eventually, through that deep OS integration, the end state is really having that ability to, through voice and through AI, you will be able to do everything that you're doing with your fingers on the screen."

Owning a Ferrari is special in itself; not many people will ever be able to say that in their lifetime. Because Ferrari recognizes its power as a special brand, it sometimes creates even more desirable models beyond the standard ones. These more special cars usually take inspiration from the past and are sold in limited numbers.

One of the more recent limited-run Ferrari cars is the SP3, built and sold back in 2025 under the “Icona” (Icon) series. These cars have since become ultra-rare and highly sought after, as shown by a recent auction sale.

A very unique SP3 has just sold for an astonishing $18.5 million during the Broad Arrow auction held in Las Vegas. This specific car was Chassis no. 314846 and belonged to a known collector through the Ferrari of Long Island, New York dealership. Only 600 SP3s were ever built, and this is 1 of them, with just 81 miles on the odometer. In terms of design, the SP3 is truly an homage, featuring the patented Ferrari horizontal slats we’ve seen on older cars, but honoring the race cars it’s based on.

The SP3 is already special, but this particular car adds its own twist to stand out even more. It’s finished in a paint palette called Verde Francesca, a lighter shade of green; that option alone costs an additional $42,185. In contrast, the hardtop, lower bodywork trims, splitter, side sills, and trunk lid are painted in glossy carbon fiber. Another key exterior detail that brightens the SP3’s look is the silver-finished rims paired with gloss black brake calipers.

Inside, the SP3 features a two-tone look: some panels use Nero Alcantara upholstery, while the doors and seats feature what Ferrari calls Mustard Aunde Jeans. Behind the driver is the car’s beating heart, a 6.5-liter naturally aspirated V12, producing 829 hp, which is the most powerful road-going engine ever and was derived from the 812 Competizione race car. As expensive as $18 million is, back in 2025 another SP3 sold for much more, at $26 million as the one-of-one 600th example of the limited series.

The SP3’s value and iconic status are also cemented by the inspiration behind the project. It was conceived as “a rolling tribute to one of the marque’s most triumphant afternoons.” In February 1967, Ferrari swept the 24 Hours of Daytona by finishing 1st, 2nd, and 3rd. The cars that achieved it, the 330 P3/P4 and 412P, became the spiritual blueprints for the SP3.

#4515. Rivian's Charging Network Grew 39% In A Year

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Rivian’s Adventure Network of DC fast chargers has expanded nearly 40% in the last 12 months, surpassing 1,100 individual chargers and 150 locations across the United States.

The company said in its third-quarter earnings report that its EV fast charging network now has 1,185 ports capable of delivering up to 300 kilowatts of power, up 39% compared to last year’s third quarter. Meanwhile, the number of stations has gone up to 165, or 26% more than at the end of Q3 2025.

The startup claims its fast chargers are powered by 100% renewable energy, though that doesn’t always mean that he electricity coming out of a charger is sourced from a photovoltaic array or a wind farm. Instead, every kilowatt-hour delivered through a RAN charger is matched with renewable sources that may operate in another town or another state.

Rivian has continued to invest in its own charging infrastructure, which uses purpose-built stalls, even though its passenger models have access to tens of thousands of public DC chargers across the U.S., including countless NACS-equipped Tesla Superchargers.

However, while the DC charging infrastructure was mentioned in the startup’s latest presentation, the Waypoints network of Level 2 chargers has gotten a lot less attention. The slower chargers didn’t get a single mention in any of the company’s most recent documents, but they haven’t been completely forgotten.

That said, the growth rate seems to have been significantly slower compared to the RAN network. According to data from the Department of Energy’s Alternative Fuels Data Center (AFDC), the company installed just ten 11-kilowatt chargers this year, with the latest pair going online in October. In total, Rivian operates 540 Waypoint Level 2 chargers at 208 locations in the U.S.

Despite the quick growth in its DC charging network, the California startup is still a tiny player in a rapidly evolving industry. By comparison, Tesla, the biggest name in the game, has over 40,000 fast charging ports at nearly 3,300 locations in the U.S., with an additional 14,000 Level 2 Destination Chargers at almost 4,000 sites.

Snowfall totals vary considerably by elevation, but the highest terrain could pick up 15 inches by Monday night. The National Weather Service also warns of gusts up to 55 mph, slick roads and visibility below a quarter mile in some areas, potentially affecting both Monday commutes.

NWS Cheyenne has a winter weather advisory for the South Laramie Range, including the I-80 summit between Cheyenne and Laramie, from 10 a.m. ET Monday to 1 a.m. ET Tuesday. It calls for 2 to 4 inches of snow in two rounds, one Monday morning and another Monday evening after a lull, with gusts up to 55 mph and reduced visibility during the evening commute.

Farther west on the same interstate, a second advisory covers the North Snowy Range Foothills, including Arlington and Elk Mountain along I-80, from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. ET Monday. That one forecasts 2 to 4 inches of wet snow and gusts to 40 mph, and the office expects roads, especially bridges and overpasses, to turn slick.

In Colorado, NWS Denver has an advisory above 9,000 feet for the mountains of Summit County, the Mosquito Range and the Indian Peaks, including the Eisenhower Tunnel, Berthoud Pass, Winter Park and Breckenridge. It runs from 7 a.m. ET Monday to 2 a.m. ET Tuesday, with 3 to 7 inches of snow and slippery roads during both Monday commutes.

NWS Billings has the northern Bighorn Mountains in Montana and Wyoming under an advisory until 10 p.m. ET Monday, with up to 10 inches of snow, gusts to 45 mph and the heaviest snow Monday morning. The office warns that snow and blowing snow will make travel along Highway 14 through the range very difficult, with visibility possibly dropping below a quarter mile.

To the south, NWS Riverton expects 6 to 10 inches above 9,000 feet in the southeastern Bighorns from 3 a.m. to 7 p.m. ET Monday, and 10 to 15 inches at the highest elevations near Cloud Peak, with gusts up to 55 mph. Granite Pass could see 5 to 8 inches, while Powder River Pass is forecast for up to 2 inches.

Wyoming’s I-80 summit faces another hazard besides snow: gusts to 55 mph that can put high-profile vehicles at risk of blowing over. The Wyoming Department of Transportation has posted closures for light, high-profile vehicles during wind events since 2011, and in 2023 it began adding specific weights to its blow-over warnings on part of I-80. That lets drivers of trailers and commercial vehicles see whether their load is at risk. Where those signs are not available, the warning reads “Extreme Blow Over Risk.”

WYDOT bases those decisions on current and forecast wind speeds along with the shape of the road, and it has found that blow-over crashes peak in winter, with the most in February and December. Restrictions show up on overhead signs and on the state’s 511 tools.

Drivers heading through the Eisenhower Tunnel should also account for Colorado’s traction law, which the Colorado Department of Transportation applies to I-70 between Dotsero and Morrison from Sept. 1 through May 31.

Compliance means tires with at least 3/16 of an inch of tread plus one of the following: four-wheel or all-wheel drive, tires marked M+S, winter tires with the mountain and snowflake symbol, or tires the manufacturer rates as all-weather. Drivers without any of those need chains or an approved alternative traction device. A standard citation brings a $100 fine plus a surcharge, and the penalty rises to $500 plus a surcharge if the vehicle ends up blocking one or more lanes.

#4513. The Karma Eximius 1 Is a One-Off Hybrid Packing a 6.2-Liter V-8

The track-ready sedan can zip to 60 mph in 2.7 seconds and wears aggressive aerodynamics and carbon-fiber bodywork.

Personalization is the latest trend to sweep the automotive world, with nearly every high-end automaker launching a specific division that caters to the needs of its wealthiest customers. Porsche has Sonderwunsch, Bugatti has Sur Mesure, and Rolls-Royce has its Coachbuild program. Now Karma Automotive, a small American brand known for slinky plug-in hybrid sedans, is launching its own program called Eximius, and has revealed its first one-off, the Eximius 1, at the Concours at Wynn in Las Vegas.

Karma Automotive, if you aren’t familiar, was birthed from the ashes of Fisker Automotive, and has sold an evolution of the Fisker Karma, known as the Revero and GS-6, on and off for most of the past decade. The Revero is a series hybrid, with a turbocharged three-cylinder serving as a generator to charge a battery that feeds electricity to a pair of rear-mounted electric motors. Although the Revero is being replaced by the new Gyesera, which further hones the same design and powertrain philosophy, this year, Karma is making sure the Revero goes out with a bang with this new one-off.

See all results for used Karma for sale near 90623

The Eximius 1 takes the Revero platform and turns it up to eleven. This special one-off trades the three-cylinder for a far more compelling engine. Under the hood lies a 6.2-liter V-8, and the plug-in series hybrid powertrain produces a total of 1195 horsepower, which is well over 600 hp more than you get in the Revero. Karma claims the Eximius 1 can rocket to 60 mph in 2.7 seconds and can hit a top speed of 200 mph. Given the Eximius 1’s more extreme performance, Karma has fitted it with carbon-ceramic, two-piece slotted brake rotors and Öhlins semi-active dampers.

The Eximius 1 is nearly two inches wider than a standard Revero, and carbon-fiber is used extensively throughout the car. Look closely at the bodywork, and you’ll be able to spot exposed carbon-fiber on the front fenders, with the blue paint fading in gradually over the carbon weave on the front doors, a truly unique finish. The Eximius 1 rides on 21-inch magnesium center-lock wheels.

Designed for driving on the track, the Eximius 1 sports a fittingly dramatic aerodynamic package. Up front, there’s a carbon front splitter, sandwiched by gaping air intakes that integrate an LED line, which, when viewed with the LED element in the headlights, creates an arrow shape pointing toward the center of the car. Two thin nostrils sit next to the headlights, giving the car a sinister sneer.

See all results for used Karma for sale near 90623

Vents have been carved into the front fenders to release air pressure from the wheel wells, and a large panel emblazoned with the number 5 incorporates a vent to extract hot air from the brakes. Below, a billet aluminum exhaust tip hints at the Eximius 1’s performance capabilities. An additional fin sits proud of the bodywork near the rear doors, and the rear end features a massive diffuser and a towering wing.

Inside, Karma has fitted blue-tinted carbon-fiber to the seats, steering wheel, center console, doors, and dashboard. The Recaro bucket seats are padded in blue Alcantara and blue leather on the bottom and Alcantara in a hue called Moondust up top. The accelerator, brake pedal, and dead pedal have been crafted from billet machined aluminum, and Karma simplified the center console to only include the necessary controls, including a red emergency kill switch.

The Eximius program will allow Karma’s customers to request modifications to the body, powertrain, and other performance components of the vehicle. Karma says it will create a maximum of nine bespoke vehicles based on each series production model that it launches. The Eximius 1 is the first, and it will be delivered to its owner in 2027.

#4512. Toyota’s Corolla Cross EV spotted for the first time [Images]

Toyota is giving its best-selling Corolla a major makeover, and an all-electric version is part of the plan. The upcoming Corolla Cross EV was captured in public for the first time ahead of its expected 2027 debut.

The Corolla has always been “a car for everyone,” Toyota’s former president and current CEO, Koji Sato, said after unveiling the next-gen Corolla Concept at last year’s Japan Mobility Show.

Since it went on sale 60 years ago, over 57 million drivers have chosen the Corolla, making it Toyota’s best-selling vehicle ever.

The Corolla has undergone 12 model changes since 1966, but the compact car is about to undergo its biggest transformation yet.

Although it’s still a top seller, the Corolla has lost some of its appeal as new, more advanced, and efficient options have emerged. Toyota looks to change that with the next-generation model.

It will remain “a car for everyone,” as Sato said, but the next-gen Corolla will come in multiple powertrains, including an all-electric version.

“Whether it’s a battery EV, plug-in hybrid, hybrid, or internal combustion engine vehicle―whatever the power source―let’s make good-looking cars that everyone will want to drive,” Sato said at the Japan Mobility Show last October.

Ahead of its expected debut sometime in 2027, a disguised Corolla Cross EV was spotted driving near Toyota’s European headquarters and R&D center.

New images from Chinese media outlet Autohome show what’s expected to be the all-electric Corolla Cross, with a closed-off grille and a unique body design.

The new Corolla will be the first to use Toyota’s new “multipathway” platform that will support electric, hybrid, gas, and other powertrains.

Toyota hasn’t revealed specifics, including battery or powertrain specs, but the next-gen Corolla EV is expected to remain close in style to the Concept. Aside from the massive COROLLA badge on the back, it looks like an entirely different vehicle with a near sports-car-like silhouette.

In an exclusive interview with Japanese media NHK in July, Toyota’s current chairman and former CEO, Akio Toyoda, warned that the company “cannot survive” if it does not adapt amid new competition and technology from China.

During the special, which went behind the scenes at Toyota’s “top secret” development site, several blurred Corolla Concept body types, including a sedan, hatchback, crossover, and GR model, were revealed in the background.

According to a recent Nikkei report, Toyota plans to begin production of the next-gen Corolla in 2028 through its joint venture with Chinese state-owned FAW Group, FAW Toyota Motor.

The Toyota Corolla EV is expected to be available in single- and dual-motor configurations with a driving range of at least 250 miles.

Let's hope that Toyota gets the Corolla EV right, because if it offers the right range for the right price but still feels fundamentally like a Corolla it is an EV that would get consideration from buyers who wouldn't otherwise consider an EV.

They're the buyers that trust Toyota and who consider the Corolla to be a nice safe choice for a car. And by safe, that means a vehicle that may not be all that exciting, but also a vehicle that they won't regret buying. Needless to say, these are not people who read Electrek, or even Car & Driver, for that matter. But there's a lot more of them than there are of us.

The hybrid version will reportedly use a new 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine and an electric motor. Toyota’s engineers told Car and Driver the system would deliver around 134 horsepower. It’s also estimated to be 10% to 20% more efficient than the current Corolla.

Toyota has yet to confirm the electric version will launch in the US. According to Car and Driver, the gas version will likely start at around $25,000, the hybrid around $27,000, and the EV and PHEVs will likely be priced in the $30,000 range.

#4511. VW’s EV Factory Is Now Taking Cars Apart. There’s Money In It

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Volkswagen has spent years converting its Zwickau factory to build electric cars, and now only electric cars roll off its production lines. But now it has received a new assignment: taking cars apart. The German plant has opened an industrial dismantling line, adding a new revenue stream.

Zwickau became VW’s electric manufacturing hub through a €1.2 billion conversion that began in 2018. ID.3 production started in November 2019, the last combustion car followed in June 2020, and the transformation was completed in January 2022 with the ID.5. Retooled production lines, extra automation, and extensive employee training now enable the factory to build six MEB-based EVs for Volkswagen, Audi, and Cupra.

The new eight-stage dismantling line will initially handle preproduction vehicles, but will eventually also handle cars at the end of their life. From 2027, it will process 4,100 vehicles annually across two shifts, employing 100 workers who were retrained for the new role. Construction and approvals took nine months, finishing three months early; VW says it could reuse manufacturing equipment to cut costs.

The automaker says it has been selling usable original parts recovered at Zwickau since July, with doors, bumpers, motors and transmission components reportedly in especially high demand. They’re available through its dealer and service networks, independent workshops and parts retailers.

The idea is to make repairs affordable enough to keep older cars on the road instead of writing them off. The dismantling line initially handles pre-production vehicles, although VW doesn’t identify which cars supplied the parts already sold. It also hasn’t disclosed prices, sales volumes, warranty terms, or how it inspects components before resale.

Material recovery is another money-making opportunity. Separating plastics before recycling helps preserve their usefulness for new components. VW says plastic recovered from one vehicle could contribute recycled material to three new cars (not all of it, though).

VW is also looking to expand its recycling business and plans to invest up to €90 million, with the Saxony government pledging €10.7 million, and it could eventually support 1,000 jobs. Zwickau has no vehicle production planned beyond 2031, though, so this new recycling line still leaves its long-term future uncertain.

That uncertainty comes as Volkswagen’s rising EV sales are putting pressure on its profit margins, because its electric models still earn less than combustion cars. The squeeze has also prompted it to pause development of the upcoming electric Golf until it can accommodate the investment. For now, dismantling remains a business whose profitability at scale needs proving, and it’s unclear if this can generate enough work (and profit) to really matter for the Zwickau plant.

VW hasn't said the operation will be limited to EVs, though, and the photos it published seem to suggest otherwise. At least one of the cars pictured (the dark blue one) appears to be a Golf, although the captions don’t identify the models. Zwickau may build only electric cars, but its new used parts business looks set to cater to a broader crowd to maximize revenue potential.

If you’re trying to stay within a budget every time your car needs work, independent repair shops can be heaven-sent. Unlike dealerships with their pricing rituals, independent mechanics often give you a fighting chance to fix your ride without spending a fortune.

However, not every shop sees things the same way. That’s why it’s always smart to get a second opinion before you green-light any wallet-busting repairs.

One Toyota Tundra owner learned this lesson the hard way. He took his truck in for a pre-road trip checkup and got hit with a repair estimate so steep it practically begged for a second opinion.

The vehicle in question was a 2016 Toyota Tundra with approximately 118,000 miles. According to the original shop’s assessment, the truck supposedly needed a replacement engine because of leaking head gaskets and valve covers. It also needed a front differential carrier assembly, with the estimate for the latter reportedly reaching $5,700. The combined bill came close to $25,000.

Enter Dave of Dave’s Auto Center, the second-opinion mechanic. He wasn’t buying it. The Tundra rolled into his shop under its own power, the engine sounded happy, and the oil level was right where it should be. No major oil or coolant leaks in sight, either.

Then there was the front CV axle. The first shop said it had too much play and needed a whole new front differential assembly. Dave? He couldn’t even get the problem to show up at first.

During a four-wheel-drive test, he eventually traced the metallic scraping noise to a slightly bent dust shield. A quick adjustment with a screwdriver stopped the noise.

He also contacted the original shop to discuss its findings, although the disagreement over the axle’s condition remained unresolved pending a more precise measurement.

After speaking with the customer, Dave concluded that the truck didn’t need an engine or front differential replacement. Instead, it needed overdue preventive maintenance, including fresh fluids and spark plugs.

He also planned to have his technicians measure the axle’s movement using a dial indicator to establish whether the play was actually excessive.

There are a few takeaways here for car owners. First, don’t automatically approve expensive repairs simply because they’re listed on an inspection report. Ask for supporting evidence, photographs, measurements, and an explanation of why a particular component needs replacement.

Second, pay attention to your vehicle’s symptoms. A truck that runs normally, doesn’t overheat, and isn’t losing coolant may warrant further investigation before an engine replacement is considered.

Finally, don’t underestimate the value of a second opinion. In this case, a customer potentially avoided a nearly $25,000 repair bill simply by having another mechanic take a closer look.

#4509. The Shelby You Never Knew Existed Is for Sale on BaT

This 1987 Shelby Lancer is no Mustang, but it, too, bears the famous signature.

For many enthusiasts, a performance-tuned Lancer is all about rally-bred heritage, preferably with the likes of Tommi Mäkinen taking the fight to Colin McRae and his blue Subaru STI in WRC action. But before the Mitsubishi Lancer, there was a Dodge, and the motorsports hero making it dance wasn’t a Flying Finn but a Texas chicken farmer.

This 1987 Shelby Lancer, up for sale on Bring a Trailer (which, like Car and Driver, is part of Hearst Autos), hails from the golden age of ol’ Shel cranking the boost on various front-wheel-drive Mopars. Not only is it Shelby tuned, but it was also actually built at Shelby’s California operations, making it just that little bit more special.

See all results for used cars for sale near 14094

1987 was the only year for the California-made hopped-up Lancers, with the later models (badged Lancer Shelby) built in Michigan alongside normal Lancers. Just 800 examples of these first-year cars were made, split 50-50 volume-wise between manual and automatic transmissions. Survivors are rare.

This example is made extra rare by virtue of its incredibly low mileage: just 1500 miles on the odometer. According to the seller, the current owner’s father traded in a 1960s Shelby Mustang on it, then drove it extremely sparingly.

From an investment standpoint, that trade might have been the best move. However, by the late 1980s, a Sixties Mustang would have been rowdy but pretty crude. By contrast, this Shelby Lancer is crammed with goodies, from air conditioning to power windows and door locks, leather seats, and even a factory CD player. That last was a pretty rare find in 1987.

The 2.2-liter four-cylinder engine features turbocharging and intercooling, and it was good for 175 horsepower and 175 pound-feet of torque. Here, the transmission is a three-speed automatic, perhaps not the purist’s choice, but at least the Shelby Lancer got the same power output no matter how the gears were shifted. Later cars were significantly less punchy with the automatic gearbox.

As expected with a Shelby car, there’s plenty of badging along with a plaque denoting that this car is number 590 of the 800 made. However, the boxy looks are pretty reserved for the 1980s, with a mild aero-look package and tasty 15-inch basket-weave rims. It looks small, punchy, and agile.

In fact, it’s so appealing that you have to think even Tommi would approve. After all, this little pocket-rocket only came in red, the same way all the best sporting Lancers did.

#4508. Tesla Powerwall 3 now boosts heat pumps to store cheap solar as heat

Tesla has launched Heat Pump Optimization, a feature that lets the Powerwall 3 and three-phase Powerwall 3P tell a compatible heat pump when to run harder so a home can bank cheap or surplus solar energy as hot water.

It’s live in Europe only. Tesla hasn’t said anything about bringing it to the US or Canada, and the hardware standard it relies on barely exists on this side of the Atlantic.

According to Tesla’s support page for the feature, the Powerwall watches electricity prices and solar production throughout the day and sends the heat pump one of two signals: run normally, or boost.

When it’s told to boost, the heat pump heats water beyond what the home needs right now, typically into a domestic hot water or buffer tank. That stored heat then carries the house through the expensive hours, when the heat pump can run less.

What triggers a boost depends on the Powerwall’s operating mode:

Tesla Energy summed it up on X last week: “Heat Pump Optimization allows your Powerwall to boost heating when there’s surplus solar or energy is inexpensive.”

There’s no cloud integration with heat pump brands here. It’s a wire.

The feature runs on SG-Ready (Smart Grid Ready), a label the German Heat Pump Association (BWP) introduced back in 2012 with 17 manufacturers. It uses two relay contacts on the heat pump to signal four operating states, from a utility block to a forced switch-on. Tesla only uses the “normal” and “boosted” recommendations.

Tesla’s requirements are pretty specific:

And there are limits. The signals are only recommendations, so the heat pump’s own thermostat settings can override them. Tesla also notes each signal has to be held for at least 10 minutes to comply with SG-Ready, and the feature drops back to normal during a power outage so the Powerwall can prioritize backup loads.

Oddly, there’s no on/off toggle in the Tesla app. Once it’s wired up, it’s on.

The math is what makes this interesting. A 300-liter hot water tank heated an extra 30°C holds about 10.5 kWh of thermal energy. With a heat pump running at a COP of 3, that takes only around 3.5 kWh of electricity to store.

So a tank most European heat pump homes already have can soak up a big chunk of midday solar without touching the lithium in the garage. That leaves the Powerwall’s 13.5 kWh free for the stuff that can’t be stored as heat.

The market is there too. Germany sold 299,000 heating heat pumps in 2025, up 55% year-over-year according to BWP, and they made up nearly half of all new heating systems sold in the country for the first time.

Tesla is also late to this. sonnen pushed a software update in 2023 that lets its sonnenBatterie run heat pumps off surplus solar, starting with NIBE units, and SG-Ready control has been a standard feature of German PV energy managers for years.

watches electricity prices and solar production throughout the day and sends the heat pump one of two signals: run normally, or boost.

Heatpumps over here have been able to do this for years already.

And it's not one of two signals. Inverter controlled HP's enables control of the effect, and not just "normal or boost".

It’s the latest Europe-first move for Tesla Energy after it launched the Powerwall 3P with a native three-phase inverter earlier this year, aimed squarely at Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. The company announced its 1 millionth Powerwall last year, and software like this is how it squeezes more value out of that installed base.

This is a smart, cheap feature, and it’s exactly the kind of thing that makes a home battery more valuable without adding a single cell.

Heat is the biggest energy load in most homes in cold climates, and water is about the cheapest storage medium there is. Using a battery’s brain to time the heat pump around solar and tariffs makes a lot more sense than discharging lithium to run a compressor at 6 p.m.

Home batteries are changing the economics of residential energy, and pairing them with solar (and smart loads like heat pumps) is the best way to get the most out of them. #4507. Polestar 2 Production Is Officially Over. A Successor Is Coming In 2027

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

The first-generation Polestar 2 is dead for good. Production of the brand’s first electric model has ended in Luqiao, China, a company representative confirmed to InsideEVs after a report from Norway’s TV2 surfaced last month.

After six years in production, Polestar’s first mass-market model sold roughly 200,000 units worldwide and set the stage for what came next. The Polestar 2 competed with the Tesla Model 3, and although it was smaller and more expensive than the American-made electric sedan, it had plenty of fans everywhere. (Healthy lease discounts likely helped.)

The European-spec Polestar 2 got its last facelift last year.

The lovable four-door electric sedan went through several facelifts, including one that significantly changed the way it drives. When the car was introduced in 2000, its base trim was front-wheel drive, and dual-motor all-wheel drive was available as an option. But in 2023, the entry-level models became rear-wheel drive, while the top versions continued to offer AWD.

More power and more range were also added along the way, keeping the CMA-based EV up to date in an increasingly crowded market. At its peak, the Polestar 2 had up to 314 miles of EPA-estimated range, which is plenty for daily use, but ultimately the Tesla Model 3’s lower price made the Swedish-designed EV a tougher sell.

In the United States, the Polestar 2 was discontinued last year, a move that seemed to foreshadow the brand’s demise stateside. While the company’s entry-level model was axed because of hiked import tariffs on Chinese-made EVs, Polestar was ultimately strong-armed to stop selling vehicles here, after a decision from the U.S. Department of Commerce denied the automaker an authorization under the Connected Vehicle Rule.

That said, Polestar continues to sell EVs in Europe and other parts of the world, and while the first-generation Polestar 2 has been discontinued globally, a new generation is scheduled to debut next year.

With a design inspired by the Formula 2030 concept, the new Polestar 2 is expected to follow in its predecessor’s footsteps as a mashup between a small sedan and crossover, though the company hasn’t confirmed what lies in store for the new model, design-wise.

The new Polestar 2 is part of the Geely-owned automaker’s plan to launch no fewer than four new models in just three years. Half of that plan has already been enacted, with the Polestar 5 grand tourer and Polestar 4 SUV already going on sale in Europe earlier this year. Next up is the new Polestar 2, followed by a small crossover, the Polestar 7.

Used electric cars now find buyers nearly two weeks sooner than used gas cars, according to a new iSeeCars analysis of more than 1.5 million one- to five-year-old vehicles. The average used EV sells in 41.9 days, while a gas model needs 54.8.

Tesla would seem the obvious leader, since three of its models rank among the five used cars with the biggest price increases over the past year. It isn’t. The fastest-selling used EV is an Audi that typically finds a buyer in under a month, no Tesla appears in the top 10, and a Toyota bZ4X and a Honda Prologue both sell faster than any Tesla in the study. The full ranking also shows a clear pattern: compact and midsize crossovers fill the top of the list, while large SUVs and pickups sit far longer.

The average used EV now sells in 41.9 days, down from 46.6 a year earlier, according to the iSeeCars study, while gas vehicles slowed from 45.7 days to 54.8. Used EV prices rose 9.8% over the same period to an average of $32,533, which now puts them $579 above the average used gas car.

iSeeCars links the shift to fuel costs, and gas prices line up with that: regular gasoline averaged $4.33 a gallon in September, the highest September average on record, according to AAA.

Used EV Prices Jump Nearly 10% After Years of Declines

Used electric vehicle prices have reversed course, climbing nearly 10% as budget-conscious buyers flock to the secondary market for affordable options.

The Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron is the fastest-selling used EV at 29.8 days, quick enough to rank third among all used vehicles. The Toyota bZ4X follows at 33.3 days, the Lexus RZ 300e at 34.3, the Honda Prologue at 35.0 and the standard Audi Q4 e-tron at 35.8. The Kia EV6, BMW i4 and Chevrolet Equinox EV share 10th place at 36.7 days.

Tesla shows up on a different list entirely. The Model S rose 22.5% to $57,862, the Model X 18.0% to $61,309 and the Model 3 15.4% to $28,931, making them three of the five used cars with the biggest annual price increases. iSeeCars does not publish how long a used Tesla takes to sell, only that none ranks in the EV top 10. Buyers are paying more for used Teslas, but the listings disappearing quickest belong to other brands.

Grouped by body style and size, the ten fastest- and ten slowest-selling used EVs split cleanly. All mainstream compact and midsize crossovers on the two lists appear among the fastest sellers, while all large SUVs and full-size pickups fall among the slowest.

Source: iSeeCars, 1- to 5-year-old used vehicles, September 2026. Segment groupings by body style and size; iSeeCars does not group models by segment. Used EV average: 41.9 days. The electric Dodge Charger (80.1 days) also ranks among the slowest.

The clearest example comes from a single automaker. A used Equinox EV sells in 36.7 days, while a used Silverado EV takes 89.1, nearly two and a half times as long, and the Cadillac Escalade IQ is the slowest-selling used EV in the study at 128.7 days. Six of the ten slowest-selling used EVs come from GM.

Luxury models break the pattern. The Q4 Sportback e-tron and the Cadillac Optiq are both compact luxury crossovers, yet the Audi sells in 29.8 days and the Cadillac takes more than twice as long. Why individual models land where they do is something the data doesn’t answer.

For anyone hunting used EV deals, the ranking offers different takeaways depending on what kind of EV you’re shopping for.

If you want a compact or midsize electric crossover, expect competition. A used Equinox EV, bZ4X, Prologue, EV6 or Q4 e-tron typically sells in about a month, and with used EV prices up 9.8% over the past year, buyers shouldn’t assume these models will become cheaper simply by waiting.

If you need an electric pickup or a large SUV, you can take your time. A used Silverado EV, Sierra EV or Escalade IQ stays on the market for roughly three to four months on average, which leaves room to compare listings before committing.

If you have your heart set on a Tesla, you are shopping the used EVs with the steepest price increases. The Model 3 still averages $28,931, below the $32,533 used EV average, but that figure is 15.4% higher than a year ago, and the Model S and Model X have climbed even more.

Tesla’s used prices are rising faster than almost anything else on the market, yet in the race for buyers, Toyota, Audi and Honda are getting there first.

#4505. Cadillac’s most affordable EV just got a bit cheaper

The 2027 Cadillac Optiq offers up to 317 miles of range, a massive 33″ infotainment screen, an NACS charge port, and now it’s a bit more affordable.

The Optiq first went on sale in 2025 as Cadillac’s entry-level electric SUV, starting at $54,390. For the 2026 model year, the Optiq arrived as GM’s first electric vehicle with a built-in NACS port and added a new rear-wheel-drive (RWD) powertrain.

Thanks to the new RWD option, the 2026 Optiq (see our review) was also slightly less expensive, with prices starting at $52,395.

While GM initially said the 2027 Cadillac Optiq would start at $52,695, prices on its website have been updated and are now slightly lower.

The base 2027 Cadillac Optiq Luxury RWD is now listed at $51,790, or $905 less than the initial price announced months ago. The Luxury AWD trim is also $905 cheaper, starting at $55,290.

Meanwhile, the Sport trim now starts at $52,395 for RWD and $55,895 for AWD, both $900 less than before.

The higher-spec Optiq Premium Luxury, Premium Sport, and V-Series trims remain at the price GM initially announced.

The 2027 Cadillac Optiq offers up to 317 miles of range in the RWD models and 303 miles with AWD. All models come with a standard 33″ Horizon Display infotainment screen, a 19-speaker AKG Studio Audio System, GM’s Super Cruise hands-free driver-assist technology, and a native NACS charge port.

Upgrading to AWD costs an extra $3,500. The Premium Luxury and Premium Sport add standard features including a Head-Up Display, ventilated and lumbar massaging front seats, and a rear cargo cover.

The high-performance 2027 Optiq-V starts at $69,295 and delivers a Cadillac-estimated 519 lb-ft of torque and 650 horsepower in Velocity MaX Mode,

How does the Cadillac Optiq stack up against the Tesla Model Y? The base Tesla Model Y RWD starts at $39,990 with up to 321 miles of range, while the AWD version costs $41,990 and gets up to 294 miles.

The Tesla Model Y Premium RWD starts at $45,990 with up to 355 miles of range, while the Premium AWD starts at $49,990 and has 327 miles of range.

Had the opportunity to drive the Optiq as a loaner while my Lyriq was in for service. I truly liked how it handled but I did find what I call a safety issue due to its design. The A pillar has an extra vertical piece and that combined with really no usable visual space forward and the side mirror create a blind spot when wanting to make a left turn on dark roads. No problem in the city where there is light. If GM would have added front side lighting when making a turn that could have been eliminated. Would have seriously looked at the Optiq for the next vehicle but that blind spot is a show stopper for me. Well that, and the fact the Optiq does not support CarPlay.

Inside, the base Tesla Model Y has a 16″ QHD touchscreen and 7-speaker audio system. The Premium model gains a 15-speaker Tesla Audio System with a subwoofer, plus an 8″ second-row touchscreen.

The two are nearly the same size, but the Tesla Model Y offers slightly more rear legroom and cargo capacity than the Cadillac Optiq.

#4504. Rivian Has Invested Millions In 3D Printing. Its Biggest Plans Are Still Ahead

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Additive manufacturing is helping automakers come up with design mock-ups faster and cheaper than ever before, and Rivian is going all in on the technology. The California startup has spent over $5 million on 3D printers, using the machines to build tangible prototypes of various parts significantly faster than going down the traditional route, which involves at least one external supplier and big, expensive stamping equipment.

But Rivian is just getting started. In an interview with CNBC, Jonathan Dankenbring, the startup’s head of additive manufacturing, said that the company doesn’t have a choice but to scale up and begin using it across all factions. “We’re going to be democratizing 3D printing for the entire company,” Dankenbring said.

So far, the R2’s maker has used 3D printers on a relatively small scale at its facility in Detroit, Michigan. The R2’s steering wheel was first printed using additive manufacturing before becoming a metal part. The technology has also been used to make electric motors for fluid testing, screw guides for tooling, stamping press inserts, and some production parts, like trim pieces, for early builds.

For the next step, Rivian is installing new 3D printers that can build flexible silicone parts. At its factory in Normal, Illinois, where its entire lineup is being assembled, the startup is adding a bay of machines, enabling employees to print parts on demand. “3D prints should be readily available for every engineer so that they can make a part and get it in their hands as soon as possible,” said Dankenbring for CNBC.

Besides the $5 million spent on 3D printers, Rivian is also paying roughly $1.7 million for the raw materials used in the machines every year. That’s quite a big sum for something that may look like big toys, but in the end, it makes a lot of financial sense for the EV manufacturer. According to Dankenbring, the cost savings have been “well in the millions” compared to traditional prototyping techniques, but more importantly, 3D printing speeds things up considerably.

By building small batches of parts on-site, the car company can lower its supplier tooling costs, cut logistics expenses, and reduce production times from weeks to days, and sometimes hours.

Rivian isn’t the only car manufacturer that has leaned into additive manufacturing. Tesla, Ford, General Motors, and many others have been using the technology to make stuff faster and cheaper, thanks in large part to the 3D printing industry’s massive advancements.

A decade ago, getting a 3D printer came with an eye-watering bill, but now, anyone can buy a machine for as little as a couple hundred dollars. The printers have also gotten smaller, faster, and more precise, enabling hobbyists and big companies to create bespoke parts in a matter of hours.

Correction: CNBC interviewed Jonathan Dankenbring, not Jared Beck. The article has been updated to reflect this change.

Described as a “huge design flaw” by one Reddit user, the issue relates to the especially wide center console, which eats into the amount of legroom. The problem affects certain owners much more than others, which seems to come down to height and/or one’s driving position. Is this a flaw Toyota should look into fixing, possibly with the RAV4’s first facelift? Let’s take a closer look.

In numerous threads on Reddit and other social media forums, owners of the RAV4 have criticized the design of the center console, which is particularly wide at the point where the driver’s right knee makes contact with it.
