#4502. How to Choose the Best Car Battery

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

Here's what you need to know to choose the right battery for your vehicle.

We've all experienced the stomach-churning trauma of a dead car battery. You need to be somewhere and you're running late. You jump in, twist the key or push the start button, and . . . nothing! Or maybe just a sickening click-click. Suddenly you need a jump-start or, worse, a tow. And probably a new battery, too. But which one?

So many brands, types, prices, and places to buy them. Which to choose and why? You don't need to be an expert to make an informed, cost-efficient purchase. Here are some brands we trust, but always check your owner’s manual for details and recommendations.

Check your owner's manual for your original battery's size, specifications, and ratings. You can also find which one you need from guides in the auto-parts store or online.

See all results for used cars for sale near 85032

Replacing a battery yourself is an option; it's not particularly difficult. Some shops offer free installation—but only if the battery is purchased from them.

If you're buying one of the batteries above online and installing it yourself, be sure to check your owner's manual for critical information before purchasing your new battery. Modern cars have specific requirements on their electrical systems, and the wrong power source could leave you stranded.

Most batteries are located up front, under the hood, where they're easy to access and replace with a couple of wrenches. But some are buried in the trunk or elsewhere—not so easy to find, let alone remove and replace.

Just remember, the negative terminal is always the first thing you disconnect and the last thing you reconnect.

Regardless of whether you're doing it in your driveway or letting a shop install, it's a good idea to first make sure you're buying the correct physical size. A number of sizes fit today's wide variety of vehicles.

For instance, size 24/24F (top terminal) batteries fit many Honda, Acura, Toyota, Lexus, Nissan, and Infiniti vehicles, while size 35 (top terminal) units fit many other Japanese vehicles, including recent Toyotas, Nissans, Hondas, and Subarus.

Size 48H6 (top terminal) batteries fit many European and American vehicles. Again, you can find which size you need in your owner's manual, in the replacement guides at the retail store, or online.

Almost all cars come with a 12-volt sealed lead-acid (SLA) battery of some variety (a few high-performance cars are equipped with lithium-ion batteries). These SLA batteries use the same chemistry as the ones your dad had to periodically top off with water, but today they are sealed—hence the name—and maintenance-free.

See all results for used cars for sale near 85032

Absorbent glass mat (AGM) batteries have quickly become the norm for most modern cars. They use similar chemistry as SLAs but are more durable and are claimed to stand up to more charge cycles.

Gel-cell batteries are best for deep discharging but may have problems in extreme hot or cold. Those old "wet cell" batteries from Dad's day are still available, though primarily for older models or penny pinchers. They are likely not offered in the right sizes and specs to support modern cars, however.

The next thing to check is the engine-cranking power of a vehicle battery, which is expressed in cranking amps (CA) and/or cold-cranking amps (CCA), a measure of how much electric current (in amperes) it can deliver for 30 seconds at 32 and zero degrees Fahrenheit. A bigger number is better, especially in cold weather, when batteries are at their weakest.

Another number to understand is the battery's reserve capacity, which is how long it can provide power with the engine off and headlights and/or accessories on or if the vehicle's charging system fails. One and a half hours is good. Two hours is better.

Also important is the warranty, which should be at least three years for full replacement (assuming no signs of neglect or abuse), plus, in some cases, a prorated refund for some time after that. Bear in mind, manufacturer warranties are often not supported when parts and accessories are purchased online from retailers like Amazon or Walmart.

Finally, be forewarned: Some brands, such as BMW, require the battery to be "coded" (digitally mated) to the car or it will not take a charge. Coding the battery requires BMW-specific OBD-II software that any reputable service shop or BMW dealer will have.

Expect to pay anywhere between $100 and $400 for a new battery, with lower-performing SLA types at the low end and stronger, longer-lasting AGMs near the top. If you're having it installed, the shop will dispose of your old battery.

If you're doing it yourself, take your old one to the retail outlet for recycling and to avoid a core charge—a mandatory deposit on your new battery that is refunded when you return the old one. Before you hand it over, place it side by side with the new battery to confirm the one you're buying is the same size. It's a final check to make sure your choice is the right one.

Oh, and if you're taking it home to install, get one with a traveling handle if possible—a car battery can weigh between 25 and 60 pounds.

#4500. Hyundai Says Hydrogen Cars Aren’t Dead. Finding Customers Is Another Story

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Hydrogen fuel cell cars were supposed to be the next leap forward in the automotive world. They drive like electric cars, but you can refuel them with hydrogen and drive hundreds of miles without having to sit at a charger for half an hour, and best of all, there are no nasty emissions.

It sounds like the perfect solution for pretty much everybody. Yet, ask anyone if they know someone who’s driving a hydrogen car, and they’ll struggle to come up with an answer. Toyota tried (and is still trying) with the Mirai, and Hyundai is still trying with the new Nexo. BMW, General Motors, Honda, and others have also dipped their toes into the technology, with varying degrees of success.

The second-generation Hyundai Nexo FCEV was unveiled in 2025, when it was touted as a global model.

But why aren’t we all driving FCEVs? For starters, there’s barely any hydrogen refueling infrastructure in place, and now a Hyundai executive has revealed that people don’t really want to buy a hydrogen car in the first place.

“The biggest thing is you’ve got to find customers, said Scott Nargar, Senior Manager of Future Mobility & Government Relations at Hyundai Australia, for CarExpert. Despite having problems finding buyers, the Hyundai representative insisted that hydrogen isn’t “dead for passenger vehicles.”

Besides having extremely limited access to refueling stations, hydrogen-powered cars are also more expensive than comparable gas and electric vehicles. That’s not exactly a good look, especially now when prices of new EVs are considerably lower than a decade ago, making them a perfect fit for those who are prepared to make the switch to electric.

What’s more, the electric charging infrastructure is now very well laid out, with even more chargers coming in the near future, making range anxiety and charging anxiety a thing of the past.

So with such easy access to electric cars, why would any company still bother to invest in hydrogen fuel cell vehicles? It all has to do with diversifying. In spite of the huge costs associated with developing a new fuel cell stack and installing refueling stations, some automakers, including Hyundai, believe that hydrogen will still have a place in the future where gas and diesel might not be as ubiquitous as they are today.

While Toyota decided to let anyone in California spend their hard-earned money to buy a Mirai, Hyundai’s hydrogen-fueled dream has been largely limited to a few real-world trials. Its latest passenger FCEV, the second-generation Nexo crossover, can drive roughly 435 miles on a full tank of hydrogen, powered by a 110-kilowatt electric motor and a 2.64-kilowatt-hour high-voltage battery that acts as a buffer between the motor and hydrogen fuel stack.

There’s a lot of debate and heated discussions when it comes to AI. One one hand, it has been an effective assistant when used right, cutting down time when it comes to delegation and distribution of tasks. It has the ability to make more menial tasks that little bit less tedious, and can speed up workflow. Again, this is if the technology is used properly.

But with any new technology, it can also be used with malicious and criminal intent. The auto industry isn’t spared from that, and fraudsters can explore new possibilities to continue their activities with it.

In a report by Car Dealership Guy, organized networks are turning to auto financing fraud by exploiting gaps in security in digital automotive retail operations. Granted, it’s not a new thing, but AI has made it easier for criminal elements to do such schemes.

Per the National Insurance Crime Bureau (NICB), more synthetic identities are being flagged, and there’s now a higher incidence of credit washing and false theft claims. Other schemes include the submission of inflated or AI-fabricated pay stubs, and automated bot attacks on dealers and retailers. Dealers have reported a 77% increase in fraudulent activity over the past two years, while 24% of default cases have some links to fraud. As for credit washing, it skyrocketed to 228% from early 2024 to mid-2025.

The NICB says it estimates that $10.4 billion has been lost through these fraudulent lending schemes, and adds that number will be even higher this year. The agency also notes that nearly 70% of its vehicle finance fraud cases inflated or synthetic identities. It’s been estimated that each case costs aggrieved parties between $22,000 and $50,000. There have also been more elaborate schemes, with one such case involving an AI-generated cloned dealership scamming a buyer out of $77,300.

Financial fraud, as a whole, lowers economic productivity as it siphons cash flow from legitimate businesses to unsavory enterpises instead. It also erodes trust in an industry, and forces industries to put up more more rules to weed out criminal elements. But, in doing so, the cost of putting up more safeguards is passed on to the consumer via operational and administrative costs.

For dealers, this may lead them asking for even more requirements for the sake of identity verification, among other things. For consumers trying to fight fairly in life, it’s going through more hoops just to be able to buy a car. In its press release, the NICB “advocates for the modernization of state and federal statutory frameworks to close gaps exploited by synthetic identity rings,” with NICB COO Timothy R. Slater saying “Vehicle finance fraud has evolved from isolated credit misrepresentations into an organized, digital criminal industry that touches dealerships, lenders and insurers. Stopping these networks requires shifting away from reactive, siloed defenses toward standardized and synchronized cross-industry reporting.”

#4498. The BMW iX is sold out, but you might like what takes its place even more

BMW is saying goodbye to the iX. With the 2026 model essentially sold out, BMW is preparing to introduce its replacement, which already looks like a big upgrade.

The iX went on sale in the US in 2022 as BMW’s first dedicated electric SUV. After a short four-year run, BMW confirmed earlier this year that it was discontinuing the iX in the US after the 2026 model year to make room for its next-generation of fully electric vehicles.

BMW didn’t take long to sell through inventory, with 2026 iX models essentially sold out in the US.

The iX landing page now redirects you to the new BMW X5 instead. According to online auto research firm CarsDirect, about 10 new iX models remain nationwide.

BMW’s Neue Klasse vehicles, starting with the new 2027 iX3, mark a step change from its previous EVs.

At the center is the Neue Klasse platform, which introduces BMW’s sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive, new batteries, and an 800-volt electrical architecture.

BMW said the new Gen6 eDrive system delivers 30% higher charging speeds and driving range than its previous system, with some models seeing an even greater increase.

The 2027 iX3 50 xDrive, BMW’s first Neue Klasse vehicle, starts at $61,500 and offers an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 434 miles. In comparison, the 2026 iX xDrive 60 had an EPA range of up to 364 miles.

While the iX3 is a smaller, compact electric SUV compared to the iX, BMW is preparing to launch the iX5 as a more direct replacement.

The gas-powered 2027 X5 40 xDrive is now on sale, starting at $72,100, but BMW is expected to launch the electric iX5 in early 2027.

A few weeks ago, BMW put the new iX5 60 xDrive to the test at an international media event in Southern California to show just how fast it can charge.

During the event, the new iX5 hit a peak of 464 kW. BMW said that with up to 460 kW peak charging, the iX5 60 xDrive can add up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes. To charge the battery from 10% to 80% takes just 22 minutes.

Using a 144 kWh battery, BMW said the electric SUV will offer up to an estimated 435 miles of range on a single charge.

The iX5 is powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, delivering a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque. BMW says it can go from 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds and tow up to 6,000 lbs.

Inside, the iX5 will be an upgrade from the iX, adopting BMW’s Neue Klasse design. The setup includes a 17.9″ navigation touchscreen and the new BMW Panoramic Vision that spans the windshield. You can also opt to add the optional 14.6″ passenger screen for a third display.

Measuring 197.2″ long, 78.7″ wide, and 68.9″ tall, the iX5 is slightly longer and taller than the outgoing iX, with more of a traditional SUV design.

BMW is expected to open orders for the new iX5 60 xDrive this month, starting at $79,800, with a full launch in early 2027. It will be BMW’s first fully electric vehicle built in the US.

Production is set to begin at BMW’s Plant Spartanburg in South Carolina by the end of the year, with the first deliveries expected in early 2027.

China sales fell 31% last quarter, yet Mercedes says it is “indispensable” and plans to build future Chinese-market cars almost entirely with local parts.

Mercedes-Benz, though currently struggling to retain market position in China, says it will give a broader 2030 strategy update, which will include a detailed review of its China business, next year. The numbers explain the urgency: German brands have been getting crushed in China.

Mercedes-Benz is doubling down on the market that is hurting it most. According to Reuters, CEO Ola Källenius calls China an “indispensable market and innovation hub.

Third-quarter Mercedes-Benz Cars sales fell 8 percent to 407,232, with China down 31 percent to 86,800, according to BigGo. Elsewhere, Europe was up 5 percent, Germany was up 13 percent, and the US was up 6 percent, with record battery-electric sales up 61 percent. Adjusted return on sales for cars dropped to 2.5 percent from 4.8 percent, and Mercedes cut its full-year guidance to 2-3 percent from 3-5 percent; its CFO called the fourth quarter “a break-even quarter.”

Starting with the electric E-Class in the second half of 2027, Källenius said Mercedes will source “almost everything” in China for Chinese production. According to reports, CFO Harald Wilhelm also wants the company to rely less on China as a profit source. That is a split-screen strategy: stay in the world’s largest car market, but with local suppliers and less exposure to its price war. Mercedes has already felt that pain from tariffs and China’s EV boom.

If you live in the US, this is the good-news part. The China sourcing applies to cars built for China, and nothing in the reporting says it changes what’s sold here. What matters more is where Mercedes is growing: US sales rose 6 percent last quarter, and Källenius said the company plans further US investments and sees potential to lift annual sales from more than 300,000 vehicles toward 400,000, per Reuters. Audi announced a $4 billion US assembly plant that will create around 4,500 jobs. Mercedes too is changing gears in a push for higher volume after years of sliding sales. For buyers, that could mean more attention and more incentives, though nothing has been promised.

In Germany, Mercedes will relaunch a voluntary severance program for indirect staff from December. It booked about €1.8 billion (about $2 billion) in provisions for the last round in 2025, with most of the new program’s earnings impact expected in 2027. Källenius said further German investment depends on productivity and costs, noting US labor costs run at roughly 80 percent of German levels.

#4494. Tesla Warned Owners Not To Test Emergency Drive Away. Some Did Anyway.

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Tesla recently rolled out a new feature that will allow owners to drive away from a Supercharger in an emergency. That feature came with an asterisk that Tesla was abundantly clear about: Don't hit it unless you absolutely need to, or else.

Well, a few owners were curious about what would happen if they decided not to heed that warning and activate the feature while plugged into a Tesla Supercharger. And now, through the magic of social media, we now know exactly what happens when an owner flips the switch.

But first, let's talk about what we know happens when a user tries to activate Emergency Drive Away. The driver first gets a warning that requires them to acknowledge the potential for damage to both their car and the Supercharger. If they choose to hit the Activate button and proceed, the Supercharger will unlock from the charge port so the owner can hit the gas and let the charging handle break away.

Again, this is for an emergency where users need to get away, and get away fast. The cost of damage to the car and the Supercharger are probably worth the owner's safety. That's why Tesla requires that any vehicle which activates Emergency Drive Away visit a Service Center so that the car can be assessed for damage before the warning can be cleared.

One owner who decided to ignore this warning was reportedly hit with a $539 fee for Tesla's service department to inspect their car's charge port. That's despite not actually driving an inch.

Another user on Reddit reported that they wanted to test what would happen "out of curiosity." They tested it in the same way—immediately putting the car in park and not driving an inch before manually pulling the charger out of the car to avoid damaging any of the equipment.

To their surprise, the car displayed an error that could not be cleared except by Tesla service and the Supercharger was pulled out of service. Fortunately, Tesla's service marked their service inspection as "goodwill" and did not charge the driver.

Another owner reported an initial estimate of $255 but ultimately left their service appointment with a $33.15 bill. A different owner was invoiced $178.20 for an inspection following their own curiosity.

Not all tests—whether intentional or not—have been without damage. Another owner on Reddit witnessed a vehicle activate the feature at a public charger and drive away.

The charger stall can be seen flexing from the cable yank and a component hit the ground behind the car, which means that driver may not be as fortunate to receive a no-cost visit to the Service Center as some of the other beta testers have experienced.

The potential bill gets even uglier if Tesla decides to begin charging for potential Supercharger repairs. Costs to the car aside, Tesla says repairing a Supercharger stall damaged by Emergency Drive Away "can be up to $25k."

There is probably room to make activation of this feature harder. But then again, Tesla may not want to make it harder to get away in an emergency. A financial penalty and mandatory post-activation service visit should (in theory) be enough to dissuade owners from activating it when they don't need to. But as we've seen from the above, that might not be the case.

#4493. Yamaha unveils new NMAX E, bringing electric power to its popular motorbike lineup

Yamaha is expanding its electric two-wheeler lineup with a much more capable machine, unveiling the new NMAX E as an electric version of its popular NMAX sport scooter.

The 2027 Yamaha NMAX E is being positioned as a 125cc-equivalent electric scooter, putting it firmly above the low-speed urban electric scooters that have made up much of Yamaha’s electric lineup thus far.

At its heart is Yamaha’s new compact eAxle drive unit, which sends power to the rear wheel through a belt drive. The electric motor produces 6.7 kW (9 hp) of nominal power and peaks at 7.5 kW (10 hp), along with 33.3 Nm (24.6 lb-ft) of torque.

Yamaha hasn’t published a top speed in the specifications, but the NMAX E’s A1 classification puts it in the same general category as 125cc combustion scooters rather than urban mopeds.

Power comes from a centrally mounted 3.5 kWh lithium-ion battery, which Yamaha says provides up to 104 km (65 miles) of range on the WMTC Class 1 testing cycle. The L-shaped battery is mounted low and centrally in the chassis to help maintain a low center of gravity.

Unlike many electric scooters that rely on removable batteries, the NMAX E uses a fixed pack. Yamaha has compensated for that with an onboard 800W charger, allowing riders to plug the scooter directly into a household outlet or an AC Type 2 public charging station. A full 0-100% charge takes around 5.5 hours.

Riders can choose between three riding modes. Sport (S) mode offers the quickest acceleration, Touring (T) provides smoother power delivery for everyday riding and carrying a passenger, and Eco (E) reduces acceleration and top speed while maximizing range. Regenerative braking is also included.

The rest of the scooter is fairly well equipped, including traction control, ABS, 245mm front and rear disc brakes, 13-inch wheels, a 33mm fork, dual rear shocks, and even a reverse mode to make low-speed maneuvering easier.

A five-inch TFT display includes smartphone connectivity through Yamaha’s Motor On app, providing turn-by-turn navigation as well as battery status, ride information, maintenance reminders, and other connected features. There’s also keyless ignition, USB-C charging, LED lighting, and illuminated underseat storage large enough for a full-face helmet, depending on its size.

Perhaps most importantly, the NMAX E looks like a proper Yamaha scooter rather than an electric experiment. Its dual headlights and distinctive side panels closely follow the styling language of Yamaha’s existing MAX family.

That could prove important as established motorcycle manufacturers increasingly attempt to bring electric models into their existing lineups rather than treating them as separate curiosities.

Pricing and exact market availability haven’t yet been announced, but Yamaha is positioning the NMAX E as a 2027 model for the European market.

#4492. Volvo Is Getting Crushed In The U.S.

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Volvo is having some trouble adapting to the fast-paced auto market changes in the U.S. From flip-flopping tariffs to the exodus of its sister brand, Polestar, there have been a ton of changes in a relatively short period of time that has been difficult for the Swedes to keep up with.

In its third-quarter earnings call last week, Volvo's leadership admitted that it was struggling to make its endeavors in the U.S. lucrative and that customer optimism in the brand has hit a point not seen in half a century.

"U.S. has proven to be a difficult market to find profitability," said Volvo's Chief Commercial Officer, Erik Severinson, during the company's third quarter earnings call last week. "The consumer sentiment in the U.S. [...] is at a 50-year low."

CEO Hakan Samuelsson said that one of Volvo's oversights was how tariffs would affect its business in the States. He admitted that the company "should have realized" that the tariffs were a real possibility and that they would need to "localize more in the U.S." to address them. The CEO went on to say that Volvo is working to address those tariff-related shortcomings to help strengthen its position in the market.

One of the long-standing ways that Volvo anticipated reversing its sales slump was with the EX60. However, the electric SUV meant to compete with the likes of the BMW iX3 and Mercedes-Benz GLC Electric has proven to be a manufacturing challenge. And with EV sales continuing to boom in Europe and other global electrification hotspots, Americans hoping to get an EX60 in their driveway will be waiting longer than originally anticipated while Europe is prioritized.

The CEO also rather publicly addressed the U.S. falling behind of EV adoption.

Without criticizing, Samuelsson noted that Volvo needs to ensure that its offerings in America would address this. Its plant in South Carolina—which is only running at 20% capacity building the Volvo EX90 (and soon the XC60)—is planned for a second new, multi-powertrain vehicle by the top of the decade.

"The U.S. is electrifying slower than the rest of the world. We need to have a new car that is also flexible in that respect, with all-electric, plug-in or hybrid," said Samuelsson.

Volvo is in a tough spot. Like many other automakers, it went all-in on electrification at the same time when other global automakers committed to building all-EV brands. But as the American market reversed course, Volvo pulled what would have otherwise been high-volume BEV vehicles (the EX30 and EX40) for the U.S. market.

The Swedes now recognize that they need to regain traction in one of the world's most important auto markets. That will come through localization to avoid tariffs, and a push for demand through multiple powertrains. Will it work? Well, that's to be seen.

McLaren’s manual-transmission McL 6GT made its global public debut at the 2026 Concours at Wynn Las Vegas, previewing a highly exclusive production supercar due in 2028.

Kia's Telluride Is Closing In On The Sportage's U.S. Sales Crown

McLaren’s first manual-transmission car in more than three decades is now out in public. The McLaren McL 6GT made its global public debut at the 2026 Concours at Wynn Las Vegas. The big news: it has a clutch pedal. The McL 6GT pairs a mid-mounted V8 with a six-speed manual transmission that drives the rear wheels. That makes it the first McLaren road car with a true manual since the McLaren F1 arrived in 1992. A production version is due in 2028.

The McL 6GT takes its name and its mission from the M6GT, the road car Bruce McLaren began developing in the late 1960s. The M6GT was based on the M6A Can-Am racer. It was meant to be the first true McLaren road car and possibly the basis for a Le Mans program. Bruce drove the prototype as his personal car, but the project ended when he died in 1970. McLaren Special Operations recently restored his original car using archive drawings, the original body molds and period photos.

The McL 6GT is built on a carbon-fiber monocoque with all-carbon bodywork. McLaren says the car is about the connection between driver and machine, not outright performance, and the hardware reflects that. It gets hydraulically assisted steering, knurled machined-aluminum controls and a gear lever tuned specifically for shift feel and throw.

The exterior borrows from the M6A: a low, wide body, a Kammback tail and a “Racing Loop” taillight motif inspired by the original M6GT. Bruce McLaren’s signature sits in the engine bay, his M6GT registration plate appears as a tone-on-tone graphic, and the “Speedy Kiwi” emblem shows up on the fuel cap and the gear knob.

Most of the segment has moved to dual-clutch transmissions and electrification, so the McL 6GT shows that a major supercar maker still sees a business case for a manual. For collectors, it’s a low-volume, heritage-driven McLaren with a 2028 delivery window. Watch for pricing and allocation details as production gets closer.

#4490. Maximo milestone: friendly robot robot has completed 300,000 tasks

After completing the first half of the Bellefield complex last summer, Maximo engineers have put their helpful robot friend into high gear, with the latest version 3.0 robot-equipped construction crews installing as many as 24 solar panel modules per hour, per person. And now, the company is reporting that Maximo has completed its 300,000th construction task. (!)

If that 24 modules per hour, per person rate sounds fast, that’s because it is. At full tilt, the latest Maximo robot-equipped crews have nearly doubled the output of traditional installation methods at similar solar locations throughout Southern California. Now, with 300,000 tasks under its belt, the robot is proving to be both fast and durable.

“The future of solar construction depends on bringing together the experience of our people and new technology,” explains Matt Tetrault, President of Primoris’ Renewables business.

Like just about everyone these days, Maximo is playing up its machines’ NVDIVIA hardware, re-branding its robots’ repetitive automation as “physical AI.” That’s not to say the robots don’t work, however – as their deployment at Amazon’s Bellefield solar field is proving.

(By) leveraging NVIDIA AI infrastructure together with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA Isaac Sim open robotics simulation framework, the Maximo team was able to develop, test and refine robotic capabilities through physics-based simulation and AI driven modeling before deploying updates in the field. The combination of AI, vision, robotics and simulation driven engineering reduced development and validation timelines and increased confidence in field performance as the robotic fleet scaled.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) powered the development, deployment, and operation of Maximo’s AI-driven field systems. AWS provides scalable computing, automated software delivery, and advanced data analytics, including real-time construction intelligence, enabling Maximo to collect operational robotics data and continuously improve performance.

The rapid deployment of solar panels at utility scale projects like this one, which is set to eventually reach over a GW of solar generating capacity, will help companies like Amazon reduce their carbon footprint, of course – but also save them big money as the price of fossil fuels continues to climb.

The Maximo team says it has plans to extend its robots potential use cases beyond solar and into construction tasks that require similar pick and place and feeding and attaching movements, site logistics, and site cleanup. And like just about every other business that demands a high degree of physical labor, the construction industry is facing huge labor shortages, making machines like Maximo that provide real efficiency gains welcome additions to the job site.

#4489. BMW's Tesla FSD Rival Hits City Streets In 2027

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

BMW's advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) is already pretty good and can smoothly cruise highways hands-free. However, BMW wants to up its ADAS game even further by expanding the system to include city driving in 2027. In other words, BMW's rival to Tesla Full Self-Driving (Supervised) is coming soon.

The navigation-guided, "partially automated" system will be able to use BMW maps to make turns, lane changes, navigate roundabouts, and even understand right-of-way situations, BMW announced on Monday. It can already handle some stop-and-go situations, and even stop for traffic lights, but this will be another step up.

"By extending partially automated driving functions to urban areas, we will offer our customers a real improvement in driving comfort—with confident driver assistance in true BMW style," said BMW board member Joachim Post in a statement. "The system will support them seamlessly along the navigation route, from motorways through country roads and into the city."

Much of the auto industry is racing to match Tesla's FSD with their own point-to-point driving systems for cities. Perhaps most importantly, BMW's perennial rival Mercedes-Benz is working on the technology with both Nvidia and Wayve. Rivian plans to launch an in-house point-to-point system to its cars next year.

BMW drivers will be able to see what the car is planning to do in BMW's Panoramic Vision dashboard. The screen in front of the driver will indicate the traffic it's seeing around itself, what it's currently doing, and all other relevant info. Since this is a Level 2 system, drivers will have to remain attentive.

Rollout for this new ADAS will start in Germany next year, with other markets following over time. (BMW didn't announce a timeline for a U.S. rollout.) The hardware for this new ADAS will be standard on several new models, like the BMW iX3, iX4, 3 Series, X5, and 7 Series. The software itself will be available via an over-the-air update, BMW says.

This subterranean garage serves simultaneously as an active vehicle storage facility, an open-concept corporate office, and a fully equipped television production studio.

Because the massive concrete room lacks any interior walls or soundproofing, conducting daily corporate business here requires some incredibly creative workarounds. When DeMuro is actively filming vehicle reviews under the bright studio lights, employees are completely forbidden from taking meetings or having loud conversations due to the aggressive echo. The Petersen Automotive Museum YouTube channel featured Doug’s garage and the inventory parked beneath the streets of San Diego is exactly as quirky as you would expect from DeMuro. While DeMuro famously drove his 2005 Ford GT across the country rather than preserving it like an 8-mile museum piece, his current personal fleet parked in the lair includes a beloved Lamborghini Countach and a worn 1999 Mercedes-Benz G500 Cabriolet. Employee Ryan Lopez’s custom “Zesty” drift car also shares the floor. Beyond the vehicles, the facility is thoroughly equipped to keep the Cars and Bids team operating around the clock, featuring a full kitchen routinely stocked with donuts, a laundry room, and a full bathroom.

When the team actually takes a break from reviewing rare Japanese imports and manual-swapped Maseratis, they retreat to a sprawling entertainment section. The hangout space includes a large putting green, comfortable couches, and an incredibly high-end racing simulator custom-built by Linus Tech Tips. The sim is even connected to a physical leaderboard, proving that even when they are off the clock, the crew never truly stops chasing lap times. Ultimately, this hidden subterranean bunker serves as the perfect headquarters for the rapidly growing auction platform, perfectly reflecting the passionate and quirky car culture DeMuro has championed for over a decade.

#4487. Former CAKE team is back in the kitchen with a new electric motorcycle

If the new ReBake Abler electric motorcycle looks like it might share a bit of DNA with Sweden’s dearly departed CAKE, there’s a good reason for that.

ReBake Motors has officially unveiled its first electric two-wheeler at EICMA 2026 in Milan, introducing the Abler as a highly modular, utility-focused electric moped and light motorcycle.

Behind the new Swedish company is founder and CEO Karl Ytterborn, who spent eight years at CAKE from its founding in 2016 through 2024. CAKE famously built some of the most interesting minimalist electric motorcycles and utility bikes on the market before ultimately collapsing after failing to secure additional funding. Ytterborn says ReBake is intended to apply many of the lessons learned during that experience, while eliminating unnecessary cost and complexity.

Its chunky 42mm aluminum tube frame isn’t just a styling exercise. ReBake designed it as a mounting system, allowing cargo accessories to attach directly to the frame at multiple locations. That means riders can configure the bike for everything from carrying groceries and passengers to more serious utility duties.

There are two versions. The Abler45 is an EU L1e-B moped with a 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed, 4 kW nominal motor and 5.12 kW peak output. It starts at €3,990 including VAT.

The €4,990 Abler80 steps up to the A1 light motorcycle category, increasing nominal power to 6.14 kW and peak power to 7.68 kW while pushing the top speed beyond 80 km/h (50 mph). Both versions use a direct-drive rear hub motor.

Energy comes from removable 2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries weighing 17 kg (37.5 lb) apiece. The Abler45 comes standard with one battery but can carry two, while the Abler80 includes two for 4 kWh of total capacity. With both batteries, ReBake claims up to 160 km (99 miles) of low-speed urban range on the Abler45 or 114 km (71 miles) on the Abler80. Each battery can be charged either on or off the bike from a normal 230V outlet, reaching a full charge in four hours.

The rest of the hardware includes 14-inch cast wheels, 140mm of front suspension travel, dual rear shocks, front and rear disc brakes with combined braking, regenerative braking, and full LED lighting.

Perhaps more interesting than any individual specification, though, is simply seeing another Swedish electric motorcycle startup emerge from CAKE’s ashes.

CAKE demonstrated that there was plenty of appetite for unconventional, lightweight electric motorcycles. Unfortunately, it also demonstrated just how difficult it is to turn that enthusiasm into a sustainable business.

ReBake appears to be getting another crack at that equation – this time with eight years’ worth of lessons already baked in.

It makes it incredible difficult to draw a line between what portion of an automaker is a car company or a tech company.

Ford would like you to know that it won't be that difficult to tell your car to zip its mouth about driver data—if it's wearing a Blue Oval on the grille, that is.

Ford also shares what it does with that data and (most importantly) how you, the driver, can turn data sharing off.

A car cannot simultaneously refuse to tell Ford where it is and also ask Ford to give it information relevant to the world around it (like live traffic data). That means if you choose to turn off connected navigation, internet connectivity, and location features in the Ford app, you'll lose some functionality within the car. And doing that would certainly make the car have a more '80s experience, after all.

The trade-off for Ford is that it uses that data to help tailor its vehicles to include features that owners want. No data means that Ford will need to find another way to customize in-car features to fit a less-connected digital experience.

Ford CEO Jim Farley also recently mentioned that the company will lean on digital subscriptions to help boost revenue with vehicles like the uber-cheap Ford Fathom. The caveat there is "digital," which means that vehicles that ditch connectivity could also be a lost cause on digital subscription revenue. And that's the ultimate compromise that owners will need to decide.

The good news is, Ford is at least being transparent about owner choice. That's the entire point according to Jones: "The trust really comes from transparency. It’s our job to be as radically transparent as we can be."

Ford and Chevrolet may be the most recognized brands in the American racing scene, but Ferrari once considered joining the fray. In the 1980s, company founder Enzo Ferrari was frustrated with Formula 1 politics and proposed regulation changes, and threatened to leave the sport. He commissioned the Ferrari 637 in 1986 for a potential entry into the CART Indy Car World Series and the Indy 500, but it never entered a race.

There was another vehicle that came out of that unusual chapter of the Prancing Horse brand’s history, which led CART entrants on the track. Well, the vehicle in question is a one-off Ferrari Mondial designed to serve as a pace car. A recent video uploaded by AVANTS on YouTube brought the pace car, now part of The Caretakers Collection, back into the spotlight, sharing some interesting bits about an American venture that never fully materialized.

The Ferrari Mondial pace car was part of the PPG Pace Car program, which fielded different vehicles at CART events, including a 1983 Dodge Daytona Turbo Z and a 1992 Subaru SVX. While the Mondial wasn’t as celebrated as Ferrari models like the Testarossa, this particular pace car has some interesting provenance.

For one, the Ferrari pace car reportedly cost $1 million to build in 1987, which, adjusted to today’s money, is around $3 million. Designed by Italian firm I.DE.A Institute, the pace car came with an extended wheelbase, redesigned front and rear bodywork, and, of course, integrated warning lights. It also featured a brake-cooling system that sprayed water through nozzles. The cabin, meanwhile, featured a custom dashboard and steering wheel, along with Kevlar and suede accents.

Powering the PPG project was an experimental 3.4-liter V8 producing a reported 300 horsepower. Forza Magazine said that the engine was being developed for the upcoming Ferrari 348. So, aside from just leading the field, the pace car also served as an early showcase for the automaker’s upcoming powertrain technology.

This Ferrari Mondial pace car isn’t for sale. But it offers a glimpse into a lesser-known era of the Italian marque’s history, especially considering the brand is better known for its strong presence in F1.

Today, the IndyCar Series uses different pace cars depending on the event, with the 2026 Indy 500 paced by the Chevrolet Corvette ZR1X. In F1, the duties of the pace car, better known as the safety car, are handled by the Mercedes-AMG GT 63 PRO 4MATIC+.

#4483. Tesla wins trade zone status for Texas Megapacks, but China tariffs stay

Tesla’s Megapack factory in Brookshire, Texas, is now officially a foreign-trade zone, a US customs program that lets manufacturers defer duties on imported parts. The FTZ Board’s approval, published in the Federal Register on Monday, runs for 14 months.

It’s easy to read this as Tesla getting a pass on tariffs for the Chinese LFP cells inside its Megapacks. Tesla’s own application says otherwise: parts hit by Section 301, 232, or 122 tariffs still pay them.

Tesla filed the request on May 20 for Subzone 84AM, part of FTZ 84 in the Houston area. That’s the factory where Tesla started Megapack 3 production in August, with a planned capacity of 50 GWh per year.

The application lists roughly 80 imported components Tesla wants to bring in under zone procedures, from coolant pumps and transformers to busbars, wiring harnesses, circuit boards and battery cells. Duty rates on those parts go up to 6.5%, while finished Megapacks and Bento inverters range from duty-free to 3.4%.

That gap is the usual reason companies set up an FTZ. A manufacturer in a zone can normally elect to pay the finished product’s lower rate instead of the rate on each imported part.

But the application spells out the limit. Components subject to duties under Section 122 of the Trade Act, Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, or Section 301 “require subject merchandise to be admitted to FTZs in privileged foreign status,” according to the notice.

Privileged foreign status locks in a part’s own classification and tariff treatment when it enters the zone. So a Chinese LFP cell that ends up in a Megapack sold in the US still pays the Section 301 tariff on Chinese non-EV lithium-ion batteries, which jumped from 7.5% to 25% on January 1, 2026. Tesla just pays it later, when the finished Megapack leaves the zone.

Here’s what Tesla actually gets out of it:

The approval came with the same wording the FTZ Board has used all year. Production was “authorized on a limited basis,” and “further subject to a fourteen-month time period.”

Tesla got an identical decision for Megapack and inverter production at Fremont, Livermore and Lathrop in California this summer, with a one-year limit instead. Eastman Chemical, battery pack maker Rose Batteries, and chipmaker Qorvo all received similar time-limited, “limited basis” approvals in 2026.

The 14-month clock puts the expiry around the end of 2027. That’s roughly when LG Energy Solution is due to start supplying Tesla with LFP cells from Michigan under a $4.3 billion contract for Megapack 3, with mass production expected in the second half of 2027.

Tesla hasn’t hidden the issue. When tariffs escalated in April 2025, CFO Vaibhav Taneja said the impact on energy storage would be “outsized since we source lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells from China.” We wrote at the time that Tesla’s only growing business was kneecapped by Trump’s tariffs.

Tesla has since brought up its own LFP cell factory in Nevada, but Taneja said it would only cover a fraction of Tesla’s installed capacity. And Brookshire alone is designed for 50 GWh a year, on top of the 40 GWh Lathrop factory in California.

#4482. Gas Vs. Electric: Which BMW Goes Further Without Stopping For Fuel?

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Range anxiety won't stop being an issue among EV buyers for a while. Customers are still new to EVs, and the entire idea of charging a car is still foreign to many people. So EV range will always be compared to gas-powered range, because that's what most drivers are used to. However, EVs are getting close and closer, if not sometimes surpassing, the range of internal combustion cars, so it's worth showing how the two different technologies actually handle the same distances. In this new video from Chasing Cars, you get to see just that: A BMW iX3 takes on a piston-powered BMW X3 in a range test.

The test was pretty simple, as the two hosts drove a BMW iX3 50 xDrive and a BMW X3 M50 xDrive from Sydney, Australia to Byron Bay. They used normal routes, kept both cars in their Eco settings, and kept the climate controls on their most efficient settings. Both cars were kept at speed limits, and both drivers stopped off if they needed to for whatever reason. So it was indicative of what a real-life road trip would be like.

From start to finish, the trip was 459.8 miles (740 km). When they started, the electric iX3 showed an estimated range of 692 km (430 miiles), so not enough to make it. But even after about 30 km into the trip, the gas-powered X3 M50 showed an estimated 784 km (487 miles) of range, which is quite a bit more than the iX3. Oddly, though, judging by the iX3's efficiency early one, the math indicated that it would make the trip with a few kWh to spare.

It's interesting to see the gas-powered car have so much more range, not because it's gas but because it's the big engine version of the X3. The M50 packs a 3.0-liter turbocharged I6, and while it's a mild hybrid, it makes 393 horsepower and 428 lb-ft of torque. It's the thirstiest of all X3s, at least until the X3 M comes out. But that doesn't make it the most powerful SUV BMW makes in this segment. The iX3 M50 is more powerful, with 463 horsepower and 476 lb-ft of torque.

Ultimately, the iX3 was able to do 747 km (464 miles) on one charge, which is significantly more than the EPA-rated 434 miles of range. It fell just 23 km (14.2 miles) short of Byron Bay. The X3 M50? It not only made it to the destination, it had 332 km (206 miles) of range left in the tank. So that clearly means it wins the test. However, the iX3 was still massively impressive, and has the sort of range few other EVs on the planet can match. So even though BMW's mild-hybrid straight-six is ultra efficient and tough to beat, that doesn't diminish the iX3's achievement.

Kia sold 80,008 vehicles in the US last month, up 16% year over year and marking its best October sales month ever.

The 2027 EV3 is Kia’s most affordable fully electric vehicle, starting at $29,890. That’s for the base EV3 Light model, which uses a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range.

Higher-priced trims, including the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT, use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.

Inside, all EV3 models feature Kia’s latest ccNC (connected car Navigation Cockpit) with standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The setup provides nearly 30″ of combined digital screens, including a dual 12.3″ instrument cluster and touchscreen infotainment, plus a 5″ climate control display.

Higher-priced trims, including the Light Long Range, Wind, Land, and GT-Line, use a larger 99.8 kWh battery that delivers up to 305 miles of range in RWD variants.

After revealing a slew of low-slung SEMA concepts last week, including a rad 300-horsepower Sentra SE-R Spec-V, Nissan is turning its attention to something considerably taller. The automaker is bringing three truck and SUV concepts to the 2026 SEMA Show, showcasing different interpretations of off-road capability and customization. One of them is the Nissan Armada Jungle Patrol, which takes the full-size SUV in a rather unconventional direction.

Inspired by rugged Nissan vehicles that have tackled challenging environments worldwide, including the Patrol, the Jungle Patrol concept is designed around the idea of an expedition-ready machine. It trades much of the Armada’s conventional SUV character for an open-air configuration, specialized off-road hardware, and a safari-inspired cabin. The result is a vehicle that looks more suited to exploring remote trails than navigating the school run.

The most noticeable change is the open-roof configuration, which removes the conventional roof in favor of a tubular steel roll cage. Nissan also fitted custom inward-facing bench seats with harnesses, giving the cabin the appearance of a traditional safari vehicle.

Under the hood, the Armada retains its direct-injected 3.5-liter VR35 V6 engine. The standard powerplant produces 425 horsepower and 516 lb-ft of torque. Nissan adds a prototype NISMO cat-back exhaust system, while Mobil 1 Extended Performance Oil is also included in the build.

The Armada Jungle Patrol is only one of three concepts Nissan prepared for this year’s SEMA Show. Nissan says these concepts are intended to inspire owners to personalize their vehicles while allowing its designers and engineers to gather feedback on potential future accessories and product directions.

The company also pointed toward its upcoming all-new Xterra, suggesting that more capable trucks and SUVs remain part of its future plans. However, none of the three SEMA builds will become production models in their current form – though Nissan says some accessories featured on the concepts may eventually be available through dealerships.

The 2026 SEMA Show runs from November 3 to 6 at the Las Vegas Convention Center in Las Vegas, Nevada. Visitors can find Nissan’s concepts at booth No. 21521 in Central Hall.

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Making the world’s fastest car comes with bragging rights, but that doesn’t mean much if safety is put second. Thankfully, that doesn’t seem to be the case with BYD’s Yangwang U9 Extreme, a Chinese-made electric hypercar that made headlines last year when it broke the 300 miles per hour barrier, securing its place among automotive royalty.

The world’s fastest car crashed hard during what looks like high-speed testing, but the driver reportedly walked out on his own without severe injuries, according to CarNewsChina. That can’t be said for the car, though. After hitting a barrier at an undisclosed speed, the two-door hypercar’s front and rear sections disintegrated, leaving just the central passenger compartment relatively intact. There were no reported battery fires.

BYD claims the U9 Extreme’s safety structure is based on a carbon fiber passenger cell designed to provide high torsional rigidity and protection in a crash. The automaker didn’t say when and where the crash occurred, but it was likely during a new speed record attempt.

In September 2025, the 2,977-horsepower hypercar hit 308.4 miles per hour (496.22 kilometers per hour), surpassing big names like Bugatti, Rimac, and Koenigsegg. But the title of fastest car in the world apparently isn’t enough for the Chinese automaker, with BYD setting its sights on the 500 kph (310.6 mph) target.

The potential run was confirmed by Stella Li, BYD’s executive vice president, who seemed confident that the mind-boggling speed is achievable in its road-going, limited-run EV. After last year’s record run, the test driver said that he could have kept his foot on the throttle for another second and a half longer, according to the data. Whether or not that would be enough to squeeze an extra 2 mph is anyone’s guess, but there’s no denying that BYD tried.

Now, it’s unclear what will happen with the automaker’s record ambitions. Just 30 units of the Yangwang U9 Extreme are scheduled to be built, and with one out of the picture, a new attempt at hitting 310 mph might be delayed.

As its name suggests, the Extreme is the most outrageous version of the U9 supercar. Sporting a 1,200-volt electrical system, Yangwang’s headline-making two-door sports car has four electric motors and a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery with a 30C discharge rate. Titanium calipers and carbon-ceramic rotors help slow down the EV, helped by a set of GitiSport e-GTR2 Pro semi-slick tires that were specifically developed for speeds of up to 310.6 mph.

#4477. This electric microcar just got a 50 mph upgrade, plus a secret Turbo mode

The adorable little Eli ZERO electric microcar is growing up. At this year’s EICMA motorcycle show in Milan, Eli Electric Vehicles is unveiling a faster, more powerful version of its pint-sized electric car, along with a sporty new limited-edition model that even includes a hidden Turbo mode.

First teased last week, the new Eli ZERO MX is the company’s first L7e-class electric vehicle, allowing it to reach speeds of up to 80 km/h (50 mph). That’s a significant jump from the 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed of the original L6e version that we originally reviewed, opening the door to a much wider range of driving scenarios.

And perhaps most importantly, the company managed to squeeze that extra performance into the same tiny package.

The Eli ZERO MX retains the original’s ultra-compact 2.25-meter (7.4-foot) length, making it considerably smaller than even the smallest conventional passenger cars.

But under that tiny exterior, the MX now packs up to 20 kW (27 hp) of peak power, compared to the 12 kW (16 hp) of the original Eli ZERO.

The upgraded model also features a 14.4 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, providing a claimed range of up to 200 km (124 miles) per charge.

That’s a pretty respectable figure for a vehicle designed primarily for short urban and suburban trips.

The rear-wheel-drive microcar features selectable ECO and SPORT driving modes, a 30% climbing capability, and a tight 7.2-meter turning circle. Charging is handled by a 3.3 kW onboard charger, allowing owners to plug in at home or use public AC charging stations.

Despite its diminutive size, the Eli ZERO MX also includes a surprisingly long list of features normally associated with much larger cars.

Those include air conditioning and heating, a panoramic moonroof, soft-close doors, keyless entry and start, electric power steering, ABS, front and rear disc brakes, and an electronic parking brake.

There’s also an 8.8-inch digital instrument cluster, a reversing camera with rear radar, and an optional 10.1-inch infotainment display with Apple CarPlay.

The MX is available in four colors: Pearl White, Arctic Silver, Graphite, and Champagne.

The biggest difference, though, is the vehicle’s classification. While the original Eli ZERO falls under Europe’s L6e light quadricycle category, the new MX qualifies as an L7e heavy quadricycle. That means it generally requires a higher-level driving license, but also allows for considerably more performance.

For drivers who love the idea of a tiny electric runabout but need something capable of keeping up with faster suburban traffic, the MX could be a much more compelling option.

Eli isn’t stopping at a faster version of its microcar.

The company is also introducing the Eli ZERO Race Edition, a limited-production model available in both the original L6e and the new L7e configurations.

Finished in an exclusive Turbo Red paint job, the Race Edition features racing stripes across the hood, roof, and body panels, along with a rear spoiler and special wheel badging.

Inside, the sporty treatment continues with a two-tone Race Red microsuede and light gray interior, including special upholstery, dashboard accents, and embroidered seats.

But the most interesting feature isn’t immediately visible.

Eli has included a secret Turbo mode activated by pressing and holding the hazard light button. After four quick chimes, the digital instrument cluster switches to Turbo mode and the car’s acceleration response becomes sharper.

Importantly, the feature doesn’t increase the vehicle’s top speed or exceed its regulatory performance limits. Instead, it changes the way the car responds to accelerator inputs, giving it a sportier driving feel.

It’s a fun little Easter egg in a vehicle that already has plenty of personality.

Eli is also offering a new Carbon Aero Kit, consisting of a carbon fiber front splitter, side skirts, and rear wing. The kit is compatible with both the Race Edition and other Eli ZERO models.

Eli has spent years developing its vision of a smaller, lighter, and more efficient alternative to conventional cars, particularly for the short trips that make up much of our daily driving.

The company has already launched its second-generation Eli ZERO, which shares the same 96V electrical architecture and aluminum chassis as the new MX.

By expanding into the L7e category, Eli is addressing one of the biggest limitations of its original design: speed.

A 28 mph (45 km/h) microcar makes plenty of sense in dense urban centers, but its usefulness quickly drops off when drivers need to venture onto faster roads. A 50 mph (80 km/h) version, on the other hand, could make the same tiny vehicle practical for considerably more people.

In the US, this could go pretty much anywhere that didn't require highway driving. Perfect one-and-a-halfth car.

The Eli ZERO family is currently available through authorized dealers in several European markets, including Italy, Norway, and the Netherlands, with prices starting at €10,500 (approximately US $12,000) for the base model. Pricing for the new MX and Race Edition hasn’t yet been announced.

Eli also has a pilot program underway in the United States, though the new models are being introduced primarily for the European market.

Both the Eli ZERO MX and Race Edition will be on display at EICMA 2026 in Milan from November 3–8.

For a vehicle that takes up less than half the space of a conventional car, the Eli ZERO is certainly finding ways to make a bigger impression!

#4476. Nissan Turns the Pathfinder into a Lifted Off-Roader for SEMA

This modified version of Nissan’s mid-size SUV features chunky mud-terrain tires and a NISMO cat-back exhaust.

In its natural state, the Nissan Pathfinder is pretty vanilla. For those who want a more rugged version, they can opt for the Rock Creek edition. And if you’re someone who dreams big and has the disposable income to turn a Pathfinder into a truly off-road-capable machine, Nissan’s new SEMA concept provides the blueprint for what its three-row family hauler can become.

The fire truck-red Pathfinder with a retro-inspired livery pictured here is called the XE-V6 concept, and it’s based on the aforementioned Rock Creek edition. It features the standard 295-hp naturally aspirated 3.5-liter V-6, which breathes through a prototype cat-back exhaust system from NISMO. It’s also outfitted with a specially made four-inch lift kit and cradle spacer to help accommodate the distinctive wheel-and-tire package.

See all results for new 2027 Nissan Pathfinder for sale near 95123

The XE-V6 concept also rolls on a set of 35-inch-tall Yokohama Geolander mud-terrain tires that have a meatier tread pattern than anything you can find in a Nissan showroom. The chunky rubber is mounted on 18-inch NISMO prototype wheels, and there’s a full-size spare mounted on the back of the Pathfinder. We’re big fans of the cool Nissan-branded mud flaps too.

To better protect the SUV’s chin and its vital powertrain components, Nissan installed a hefty front skid plate, complete with an integrated Warn M800S winch, that pairs with similarly sturdy underbody skid plates. A custom high-clearance front bumper will help the Pathfinder XE-V6 crawl over obstacles it finds in its path, and seeing those obstacles at night is made easier with the two six-inch fog lights, also courtesy of NISMO. The light show continues with the four-inch prototype units mounted on the A-pillars. Other custom add-ons include rock rails and a rear bumper that increases the departure angle and incorporates tow hooks and a trailer hitch.

Nissan doesn’t get crazy with the Pathfinder concept's interior, so all of the expected comfort and creature features remain. However, it does make extra room for storage thanks to roof-mounted accessories such as a rack with a NISMO storage case and four six-inch off-road lights. There’s also a custom MOLLE panel that hangs over the rear window and hosts a 1.75-gallon RotoPax canister. Oh, and if you need to keep some sandwiches or soda pops cool while you’re out gallivanting on trails, NISMO provides a white 45-quart ice box in the cargo area.

#4475. Ringbrothers Just Made the Ultimate Pontiac GTO

Mercedes Sales Plunge 31% in China as It Eyes Bigger US Push

Car Loan Fraud Is Costing Billions As AI Makes Scams Harder To Spot

New Toyota RAV4 Has A Comfort Issue Some Owners Can't Ignore

More than 5,500 hours of fabrication went into transforming this 1965 Pontiac into a wider, more powerful, and thoroughly reworked machine.

Ford Crams The Most Powerful OEM Crate Engine Ever Made Into New Bronco Concept

Mercedes-Benz Wants To Blow Snow Off Your Car Before You Open The Door

Shaq Spent $1.3 Million on 3 Rolls-Royces to Spite a Salesman

Two Porsche 911s at SEMA Ditch Their Flat-Sixes for Ferrari and Chevy V8s

The Pontiac GTO is one of those cars everyone knows, and for good reason. It helped kick off the muscle car craze in the ’60s, and its impact is still felt long after the original left the scene.

With a name like that, you just know someone had to give it the restomod treatment. Enter Ringbrothers and their latest wild idea: Billie. This one started out as a humble 1965 Pontiac Tempest Convertible before getting the full transformation.

Ringbrothers, based in Wisconsin, has a reputation for going all-out on their builds. These are the folks behind the 805-hp Aston Martin DBS-based Octavia, just to name one. Now they’ve set their sights on Pontiac muscle, and the result might just be the wildest GTO we’ve seen.

This project ate up more than 5,500 hours, packed with metalwork, fabrication, and some serious engineering wizardry.

The first thing you’ll notice is the bodywork. Ringbrothers stretched the car five inches wider, gave it reshaped front fenders, beefed-up rear quarters, and longer rocker panels. Carbon-fiber doors and a bunch of custom panels round out the look.

Jim Ring says the team obsessed over getting the lines just right, making sure the mods looked natural and not overdone. With a car like the GTO, keeping that classic shape is half the battle.

The whole thing is finished in a custom color called Billie Goat Blue, with shiny chrome and black accents. Custom bumpers, a billet aluminum taillight panel, and a carbon-fiber diffuser with built-in exhausts complete the package.

Inside, it’s just as wild. The dash is pushed four inches forward and dropped two inches for more space up front. You get new aluminum trim, a digital display, and even the original radio reworked with Bluetooth.

One quirky touch: the custom shifter is inspired by an olive wood espresso portafilter. It’s a weird choice, but somehow it works with the hand-built vibe.

Under the hood, there’s a supercharged 6.2-liter LT4 V8 from Wegner Automotive, good for 650 horsepower and 650 lb-ft. That’s a massive jump over anything the original GTO ever dreamed of. All that power goes through a Bowler 10-speed auto. Ringbrothers even built a custom exhaust with Flowmaster bits, so it sounds as mean as it looks.

Underneath, Billie sits on a Roadster Shop Fast Track Stage III chassis with FOX coilovers and six-piston Brembos. HRE G-Code wheels – 19s up front, 20s out back – are wrapped in sticky Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2s. All this should make Billie handle way better than any stock GTO, especially with all that LT4 muscle under the hood.

If you’re hoping to buy Billie, you’re out of luck – this one’s headed to a private owner after its 2026 SEMA Show debut in Las Vegas. No word on price, but with over 5,500 hours sunk into it, you can bet it wasn’t cheap.

#4474. Zero Motorcycles unveils $8K electric motorcycle, street-legal dirt bike, and much more

Zero Motorcycles is celebrating its 20th anniversary with a major wave of announcements at EICMA 2026, unveiling several new electric two-wheelers alongside some important technology upgrades that could make its existing motorcycles even more appealing.

The biggest news is an entirely new lightweight electric street motorcycle known as Project Ventura, designed to bridge the gap between the increasingly popular world of electric bikes plus lightweight e-motos and the full-size electric motorcycle market. But that’s far from the only news coming out of Zero’s booth in Milan.

The electric motorcycle maker is also announcing a new street-legal version of its XE electric dirt bike that was previously only street-legal in Europe, introducing its LS3 electric scooter to Europe, introducing a redesigned smartphone app, and sharing more details about its upcoming DC fast-charging system.

There’s quite a bit to unpack here, so let’s get into it.

Perhaps the most exciting announcement is Project Ventura, a new lightweight electric motorcycle that Zero hopes will attract an entirely new generation of riders.

With supermoto-inspired styling, 17-inch wheels, and a more approachable design than the company’s larger street motorcycles, Ventura appears aimed squarely at riders who want something more substantial than a typical lightweight e-moto but aren’t necessarily looking for a full-size, high-performance motorcycle.

And with a targeted price of less than US $8,000, it could be one of Zero’s most accessible street motorcycles yet.

The bike features a new electric powertrain producing over 20 kW (27 hp) of peak power, delivering a sustained top speed of 65 mph (105 km/h) and a momentary maximum speed of 81 mph (130 km/h).

That’s a particularly interesting distinction, as it positions the bike as being able to briefly reach highway-capable speeds with the occasional burst of extra performance, but perhaps not for longer sustained highway stretches.

Importantly, we don’t yet know the battery capacity, though Zero is giving us a hint by publishing a range estimate. The company is quoting an estimated real-world range of 93 miles (150 km), but without a real battery capacity figure to parse, it’s hard to take that range estimate at face value.

We do know that the bike will feature onboard Level 2 charging, allowing riders to plug into public AC charging stations without carrying around a separate external charger – something more common on the smallest of electric motorcycles that attempt to cut down on weight and cost by using an off-board charger.

Other features include standard ABS, Bluetooth connectivity, integration with Zero’s upcoming smartphone app, and a chassis designed to accommodate a passenger.

The riding position is upright, and the bike’s supermoto-inspired geometry is intended to deliver agile handling and a playful riding experience.

Perhaps most interestingly, Zero isn’t hiding the fact that it sees the explosion of e-bikes and smaller electric motos as a potential gateway to motorcycle ownership.

“When we set out to build Project Ventura, we had three guiding principles: first, build a bike so good-looking you’d want its poster above your bed. Second, make it a proper electric motorcycle that feels like a natural next step for the millions of riders who’ve spent the last four or five years on e-bikes and e-motos. And third, make it ridiculously fun to ride,” explained Jim Callahan, Zero’s Chief Product and Partnerships Officer.

That’s a notable strategy for a company that has historically focused heavily on higher-performance electric motorcycles. However, the launch of Zero’s smaller Sur Ron-style electric dirt bikes last summer showed that the motorcycle maker did see the writing on the wall in terms of the success of the e-moto market compared to larger flagship bikes.

Instead of trying to convince existing gasoline motorcycle riders to make the electric switch, Zero is increasingly looking toward younger riders who may have already fallen in love with electric two-wheelers and are ready for something faster and more capable.

But for those interested in the new Ventura, they’ll have to wait just a bit longer. The motorcycle is expected to become available in summer 2027.

Another major announcement is a new street-legal version of Zero’s XE electric dirt bike.

The original XE was introduced as part of Zero’s more affordable X Line of lightweight electric off-road motorcycles, offering a more accessible entry point to the brand than its traditional street and dual-sport models. While the model was available in street-legal format in Europe, the US versions were purely off-road affairs.

Now Zero is taking that same general concept and making it legal for public roads, opening up significantly more riding possibilities.

The new XE is fully homologated and features the necessary street equipment, including a headlight, taillight, and centrally mounted dashboard. A small integrated flyscreen and black bodywork give the motorcycle a more refined appearance, while wide dual-sport tires help it transition between pavement and dirt.

Zero has also revised the gearing, using a rear sprocket designed to balance off-road performance with the higher speeds required for street riding.

The result is a claimed top speed of 60 mph (97 km/h), making the XE capable of considerably more than simply putting around the neighborhood, though with a slight torque sacrifice.

For riders who live near off-road riding areas, the appeal is obvious. Instead of loading a dirt bike into a truck or trailer to reach the trails, owners could potentially ride directly from home to the trailhead, provided local regulations allow it.

That’s a particularly useful capability for a lightweight electric dirt bike, where much of the appeal comes from its simplicity, low maintenance, and ability to explore places that larger motorcycles might struggle to reach.

The new street-legal XE is expected to launch in spring 2027, with pricing starting at US $6,295.

Zero is also expanding its electric scooter offerings with the European debut of the LS3, a faster and more capable scooter designed for urban transportation and longer commutes.

While Zero has traditionally been associated with electric motorcycles, its growing interest in scooters represents another effort to reach riders who prioritize everyday transportation over outright performance.

The LS3 offers a top speed of 75 mph (121 km/h), which puts it well beyond the typical low-speed urban electric scooter category.

Zero also quotes a range of up to 93 miles (150 km), powered by a battery system consisting of three onboard batteries with a combined capacity of 5.6 kWh.

Interestingly, one of those batteries is removable and located beneath the seat. Riders can remove it to free up additional storage space, offering some flexibility between maximum battery capacity and cargo-carrying convenience.

That could prove useful for commuters who don’t always need the scooter’s full range but would appreciate extra room for everyday items.

The LS3 also comes equipped with heated grips and a heated seat, features that should be particularly welcome to European riders commuting through colder months.

Connected technology rounds out the package, including compatibility with Zero’s upcoming smartphone app.

The LS3 is expected to become available in Europe in spring 2027.

Beyond the new vehicles, Zero is also working on a redesigned smartphone application that promises to give riders considerably more control over their motorcycles.

The new app is being developed for the LS3, 2027 Street and Dual Sport motorcycles, and Project Ventura.

One of the more interesting features is the ability to customize riding modes. In addition to preset modes that adjust power delivery and regenerative braking, riders will be able to create a custom mode and individually tune parameters including speed, power, torque, and regeneration.

The app will also include a charging-station finder, allowing riders to search for nearby chargers and filter them by charging speed, network, and availability. Apple Maps integration will provide route guidance to selected charging locations.

An optional ride-history feature can automatically record trips, including their distance, duration, and route previews.

Riders will also be able to customize their motorcycle’s dashboard layout, choosing which information appears in each quadrant of the display.

Battery management is getting some attention, too. The app will provide controls for scheduled charging, target charge levels, charging limits, and long-term battery storage settings.

Zero is also adding integrated feedback and support tools that allow owners to report problems or suggest improvements directly through the app, including photos and diagnostic logs.

The redesigned app is expected to arrive in 2027.

Perhaps the most consequential technology announcement, at least for riders who want to take their electric motorcycles beyond short commutes and weekend rides, is Zero’s continued development of DC fast charging.

Zero says it is targeting a 2027 launch for its new fast-charging system, which will support compatible Street and Dual Sport motorcycles.

The system is being designed to charge compatible batteries from 20% to 80% in less than 30 minutes.

That’s a major improvement in convenience compared to the longer AC charging stops that have traditionally been associated with Zero motorcycles.

Importantly, the company is developing the system for both North America and Europe, with different charging connectors for each market.

European motorcycles will use the CCS standard, while North American models will feature NACS connectors.

The latter is particularly interesting given the growing adoption of NACS charging infrastructure across North America, potentially making it easier for electric motorcycle riders to access a wider range of charging locations.

Zero is also developing a retrofit option for eligible existing motorcycles, meaning some current owners may eventually be able to upgrade their bikes rather than purchasing entirely new models to take advantage of the technology.

The company hasn’t yet announced pricing or a complete list of compatible motorcycles, and the retrofit option remains under development.

Still, the prospect of adding significantly faster charging to existing electric motorcycles could be an important development for the brand.

There are several exciting announcements here, but I think the biggest takeaway is that Zero seems to be increasingly focused on making electric motorcycling more accessible through smaller and more affordable options.

For much of its 20-year history, Zero has been a pioneer in the electric motorcycle industry, often offering impressive performance and technology, but at prices that made its motorcycles difficult for many riders to justify. The bikes have long won acclaim, but $20k was a big ask.

The company’s more affordable X Line bikes have already demonstrated that Zero is interested in attracting riders who might never have considered one of its larger electric motorcycles. The street-legal XE takes that concept a step further, and Project Ventura could be an even more important addition.

I’m particularly intrigued by Zero’s explicit acknowledgment that millions of people have spent the last several years riding e-bikes and smaller electric motos, and that many of those riders may be ready to graduate to something bigger.

That’s an audience I’ve been watching grow for years. These are riders who are already comfortable with electric drivetrains, who appreciate the simplicity of twist-and-go riding, and who don’t necessarily have any attachment to gasoline engines or traditional motorcycle culture.

For those riders, a lightweight, fun electric motorcycle capable of 81 mph and priced below $8,000 could be an awfully compelling next step.

The new street-legal XE is similarly exciting, especially for riders who want to combine urban transportation with off-road adventures without needing a truck to haul their bike around.

During the late 60’s to the early 70’s the in thing in motorcycles was the street legal dirt bike. I had a 1971 model Kawasaki 125 street legal dirtbike that I bought for $525 and it was great for getting around as a kid. When this street legal type of bike goes below $5000 it could be the next big thing.

And while the new motorcycles are likely to get most of the attention, I wouldn’t overlook the DC fast-charging announcement. Charging speed has long been one of the biggest limitations facing electric motorcycles, particularly for riders interested in longer trips. A sub-30-minute charging stop isn’t quite gasoline-level convenience, but it’s getting much closer to something that can work for real motorcycle touring.

Of course, several important details remain unknown, and we’ll have to wait until 2027 to see how these products and technologies perform in the real world.

But taken together, these announcements suggest Zero is making a serious effort to expand beyond its traditional audience and build electric motorcycles for a much broader range of riders.

And after two decades of helping pioneer the electric motorcycle industry, that’s exactly the kind of evolution I’d like to see.
