#4457. Used EVs Are Selling Like Hotcakes. The Fastest Movers May Surprise You

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Used EVs are getting more popular. Not only are they increasing in popularity, they're selling even faster than their hybrid and even gasoline counterparts, according to iSeeCars.

You might assumed that all of the used Teslas hitting the market would be a big reason why. But in reality, no Tesla even cracked the top 10 list of best-selling used EVs in September 2026.

Compared to the same month last year, this September saw a 9.8% price increase for used EVs. That's exactly double the 4.8% increase used hybrids saw year-over-year. However, both absolutely crush used gas car values, which only jumped 0.3%. You can bet that high fuel prices over the past year or so have had an affect on gas and diesel demand. People are thinking about EVs more than ever before, especially every time the see eye-watering receipts from every fill up.

“These pricing shifts reflect significantly different year-over-year trends across drivetrains,” iSeeCars Executive Analyst Karl Brauer said in a release. “Ongoing higher fuel prices are likely driving the shift, though the EV segment has also recovered from the demand turbulence caused by the loss of federal incentives a year ago.”

Price isn't the only indicator of demand, though. Speed is another. Used EVs fly off the figurative shelves faster than gas cars, spending an average of 41.9 days on the lot. Not only is that 10.1% faster than September 2025, but it's almost two weeks faster on average than gas cars, which take 54.8 days to sell. Furthermore, gas car sale time increased by 19.9%. So it's getting harder to sell used gas cars, while EVs are getting easier.

Admittedly, in defense of gas cars, customers are spoiled for choice. There are far, far more gas cars available for sale—for example, Autotrader lists 1,384,383 used gas and diesel cars nationwide, but only 44,434 used EVs. There are also fewer EV models for sale, so customers aren't cross-shopping as much. Still, there's no denying that used EV demand is increasing as supply continues to grow.

There are also more options than ever in a market that was once essentially wholly dominated by Tesla. But in September, none of the top 10 fastest-selling used EV models were Teslas. There weren't any Lucids or Rivians in there, either. The quickest-selling EVs were oddly the Audi Q4 E-tron Sportback, followed by the Toyota bZX4, and Lexus RZ 300e. So it seems that used EV customers are becoming like everyone else: they just want something small and practical, with some quirky styling and a nice interior. Also on the list were the Honda Prologue, BMW iX, and even Polestar 2.

The slowest-selling EVs aren't exactly surprising, though, as they're mostly massive and expensive SUVs and trucks. The Cadillac Escalade IQ was the slowest-seller by a huge margin, but it's also uber-expensive. It was followed by the GMC Sierra EV, Chevy Silverado EV, and the Volvo EX90. The Hummer EV was on the list, too, proving that GM's Ultium trucks aren't exactly popular on the used market.

One of the reasons why used Teslas might not have sold as quickly as other EVs is that their prices have increased. The Tesla Model S and Model X both saw used price increases of 22% and 18%, respectively. That is good for the two highest of any used car on the market, regardless of powertrain.

It's interesting to see used EVs increasing in selling speed, showing that customers are willing to go electric when the vehicle type and price suits their needs. And now that data has come out proving that EVs don't lose as much range over time as previously thought, it seems that used EVs are becoming better and better buys.

Admittedly, the thought of blasting over the hedged lanes near Ariel’s rural base in Somerset, England, is more than a little intimidating. Yet even as the 4RR accelerates ferociously and telegraphs mechanical and road-surface detail like few other cars can, the big surprise is just how calm this extreme Atom feels.

Whether it’s the car’s refusal to be upset by midcorner bumps and awkward road cambers, or the drivability of the highly boosted turbo four, there’s an unexpected maturity and polish at play here. Even the Quaife six-speed sequential transmission can be soothed with a gentle brush of the clutch pedal. A handful of miles in, and our trepidation has already melted away.

Two things explain the 4RR’s fine road manners. The first is the clearly accomplished setup work overseen by race driver and former Top Gear Stig Phil Keen, and the second is some very expensive engineering.

The latter element includes reworked manually adjustable Öhlins dampers—which allowed Ariel to soften the inboard, pushrod-operated suspension—alongside a new aerodynamics package and 12.2-inch AP Racing brakes with four-piston calipers all around.

But the biggest investment involves the engine. Ariel doesn’t typically touch engine internals, but the 4RR’s previous-generation Civic Type R K20C unit has been completely reworked, blueprinted, and balanced in a process said to consume around 100 hours. Upgrades include forged connecting rods and pistons, closed-deck sleeves, and a revised cylinder head with improved camshafts, valve springs, and guides. A larger turbocharger runs nearly 25 psi of boost and is fed by an intercooler about twice the size of the 4R’s.

See all results for used cars for sale near 33157

The marquee numbers: 525 horsepower at 8200 rpm and 406 pound-feet of torque at 5200 revs. However, two tamer performance maps let you ease into it; there’s a 4R-matching 400-hp tune, as well as an intermediate 500-hp setting. Traction control and ABS are included and very welcome, both being driver adjustable through multiple stages, including fully off.

For such a small turbo four capable of producing so much power, the 4RR is disarmingly flexible at low revs and surprisingly progressive when it comes on boost, partly thanks to peak torque arriving at a far higher engine speed than in most modern turbocharged road cars.

That’s true in both the first two engine maps (despite the very noticeable step up in performance, including the intermediate map’s more substantial midrange boost), but it’s the seemingly modest 25-hp increase to the third and most powerful tune that transforms the experience. Still progressive and really quite tractable, it’s the searing, angry spit toward the 8200-rpm rev limiter that’s most noticeable, along with equally furious overrun pops. Throw in a few full-throttle, clutchless upshifts, and this amounts to delirious performance that—while usable on the road—is best reserved for an open racetrack.

Even then, traction from the 255-section rear tires is astonishing, at least in the hot, dry conditions of our drive. Whether launched off the line or subjected to a surge of midrange torque, the 4RR simply digs in and grips, thanks in no small part to compliant damping, sticky Yokohama A052 track-oriented rubber, and the weight of that Honda four pressing the rear tires into the tarmac.

Back-to-back drives in the 4RR and one of the first Atoms underlines the comedic jump in performance, but it’s the finesse of the 4RR chassis that’s more revealing of the car’s quarter century of development. Delightfully tactile as the original is, each individual wheel jiggles over bumps, and the car quickly becomes unstable if you back out of the throttle midcorner.

The 4RR retains comparable tactility but dials out the chassis noise and lifts the Atom’s capabilities to another level. The steering is super responsive but refuses to tug over tricky surfaces, the car’s balance is throttle adjustable but more forgiving of midcorner lifts, and crushing braking performance tames the engine’s power without causing the front axle to weave. For a circuit-optimized machine, the 4RR is exceptionally fluid on the road.

It’s easy to get caught up in the 4RR’s extreme nature and its hypercar-like power-to-weight ratio, but the real takeaway is how thoroughly Ariel has harnessed its intensity, creating a car that feels engineered around its performance, not overwhelmed by it.

For many enthusiasts, the best cars of all time have already been made, and no amount of modern technology can replace the mechanical simplicity of driving a classic sports car. The problem has always revolved around keeping a 30-year-old car maintained, particularly as parts become scarce. Acura has addressed this concern for owners of the original, first-generation NSX. The automaker has officially launched the Honda Heritage Parts program in the U.S., with over 3,000 reproduction parts now available for the iconic sports car.

The new program first became available in Japan in April, but Honda has delivered on its promise to expand it to other regions. The new Honda Heritage Program will support various Acura and Honda performance models, with the original NSX—produced between the 1991 and 2005 model years—being the first beneficiary.

For now, owners of the NSX can choose from over 3,000 reproduction parts, which are available via Acura dealerships nationwide. As reliable as the original NSX is—some examples have comfortably exceeded 300,000 miles—any car that old will require significant upkeep as mechanical components, rubbers, and plastic parts age.

“Honda Heritage Parts was created to help our customers enjoy their classic Acura and Honda performance models, and it’s appropriate that we begin with an iconic model like the first-generation Acura NSX,” said Mamadou Diallo, executive vice president at American Honda Motor Co., Inc. “By supporting our customers in preserving the legacy of the NSX, we’re celebrating our shared passion for these iconic sports cars and keeping them on the road for today’s enthusiasts and future generations.”

Parts can also be purchased through the Honda DreamShop. Here, customers can already find thousands of parts for the NSX’s engine, transmission, chassis, and more.

Honda is Giving a Second Life To Owners of Its Coolest Sports Cars

Honda is reviving support for its most beloved sports cars, helping owners keep iconic models running longer than ever.

Although the second-generation Acura NSX was an accomplished hybrid sports car, it never quite captured the magic of the original. The first NSX debuted at the Chicago Auto Show in February 1989 before going on sale as a 1991 model. An innovator from the start, it was the first production car with an all-aluminum chassis and body, which weighed 40% less than steel.

That first NSX had a 3.0-liter V6 engine producing 270 horsepower and 210 lb-ft of torque. With the advanced VTEC system making its U.S. debut on an Acura model, the car reached 60 mph in under six seconds, and the driver was involved in the process all the way thanks to the standard five-speed manual gearbox.

The hand-assembled NSX’s low, sleek design has stood the test of time, and high Japanese quality standards made it a car that could be enjoyed for many years without breaking down. Incrementally improved over the course of its extended production run, the NSX eventually gained a larger 3.2-liter V6 with 290 hp.

Cumulative U.S. sales of the NSX reached 8,733 units, and well-kept examples demand six-figure prices today.

The new Honda Heritage Program will make it infinitely easier for NSX owners to enjoy their cars for many more years to come. Using original, high-quality parts means these cars can perform at their best.

Over the next few months or years, there are many legendary Honda/Acura models we expect to be included in this program. One obvious candidate includes the Honda S2000, as the oldest versions of this high-revving sports car are now over 25 years old. Earlier generations of the Honda Prelude as well as sporty variants of the Acura Integra/RSX are also likely to make the cut at some stage.

#4454. Hyundai’s electric SUV finds some footing, with IONIQ 5 sales topping 33,000 in 2026

The Hyundai IONIQ 5 remains one of America’s most popular EVs outside Tesla, with October sales up 21%.

While the Tesla Model Y and Model 3 still dominate the US electric vehicle market, accounting for about 50% of all sales through the third quarter, it was the Hyundai IONIQ 5 that ranked third.

The market has slowed since the $7,500 federal tax credit was removed last September, with several automakers reporting fewer EV sales than in 2025 when buyers rushed to claim the credit.

Hyundai responded by cutting prices on the 2026 IONIQ 5 by up to nearly $10,000 on some trims, with a new starting MSRP of around $35,000.

As the market shows signs of recovery, IONIQ 5 sales bounced back in October, rising 21% to 1,981 units.

Through the first 10 months of 2026, Hyundai sold 33,093 IONIQ 5s in the US, still down 23% from the more than 42,700 it sold during the same period last year, when credit was still available.

Hyundai said the IONIQ 5 helped drive growth as the company posted its best October in the US ever with 73,452 vehicles sold, a 5% increase YOY.

While Hyundai sold only 169 IONIQ 9s last month (-47%), sales are still up 49% through October, with nearly 6,700 units sold.

Hyundai’s hybrids set a new October sales record, rising 20% from last year and accounting for 29% of total sales in October. Through October, Hyundai’s total US sales are up 3% YOY at 770,916 units.

Since not all automakers report monthly sales figures, it’s hard to determine where the IONIQ 5 stands through October.

Earlier today, Hyundai’s sister brand Kia reported that sales of its three-row electric SUV, the EV9, were up 11% year over year in October. EV9 sales are now up 5% year-to-date, with 13,835 units sold through October.

The cheapest 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 SE Standard Range starts at $35,250 and offers up to 245 miles of range.

If you want more range, upgrading to the extended-range SE RWD model costs an extra $2,500, but you get up to 318 miles of range on a single charge.

#4453. Pennsylvania is way ahead on NEVI charging – now comes another $37M

Pennsylvania is putting $37 million in federal NEVI funding toward what PennDOT says will be 515 new public EV charging ports across the Philadelphia region, including curbside chargers.

The awards cover Bucks, Chester, Delaware, Montgomery, and Philadelphia counties. PennDOT says the projects will expand public charging availability by 27% across the region and 53% in Philadelphia.

For drivers without a driveway, curbside charging gives them somewhere to plug in while parked near home.

It’s Electric PA received $2.93 million for 157 on-street Level 2 ports across 13 Philadelphia neighborhoods. Voltpost received funding for another 62 curbside ports across the four suburban counties.

Fast charging is getting funding, too. PositivEnergy received $7.2 million for 54 DC fast-charging ports at 11 Philadelphia Parking Authority lots. Tesla received two $392,000 awards for eight ports each at Royal Farms in Broomall and Wawa in Plymouth Meeting.

The money comes from the federal National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) program, created by the Biden administration’s Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. Pennsylvania’s five-year allocation is $171.5 million.

NEVI initially focused on fast charging along designated highway corridors. States can spend the money more broadly after the Federal Highway Administration certifies that their corridor charging requirements have been met. Pennsylvania received that certification on September 22, 2025.

In fact, Pennsylvania has built 54 EV charging stations using NEVI funds so far – more than double the number of any other state.

PennDOT’s community charging program supports both Level 2 and DC fast charging. Its published program minimum requirements include at least four ports per proposed station, at least 6 kW per port, two ADA-compliant parking spaces, and J1772 or CCS connectors on every port. Equipment must also meet Buy America requirements.

PennDOT lists 71 awards in this southeastern round as part of its roughly $100 million statewide community charging effort.

Applications for the western region close November 20. Central and eastern Pennsylvania applications close March 12, 2027.

For the southeastern projects, PennDOT’s estimated schedule puts environmental reviews in November 2026 through January 2027, followed by agreement execution in January and February. Drivers will still have to wait for construction and commissioning before these awards become places to plug in.

The Mazda3 remains one of the more affordable new cars available in the United States, and it happens to be one of the more enjoyable compact cars to drive, too. It’s a reasonable case for buyers who want something more engaging than an ordinary commuter car without spending too much.

#4450. BYD’s flagship luxury EV with 1,000+ km of range hits 4,000 sales in just 19 days

BYD wasted no time, with sales of its new flagship electric sedan reaching 4,000 in just 19 days since its launch.

With a record of more than 300,000 electric vehicles sold last month, BYD sold more EVs than the US did in the entire third quarter, combined.

A big part of the higher demand is thanks to BYD’s latest breakthrough technology, including its second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging technology.

BYD began equipping vehicles with the new battery and charging tech in March, and over the past six months it has posted higher year-over-year sales growth. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 vehicles, up 6% compared to the same period in 2025.

On October 13, BYD launched the Great Han, or “Da Han” in China, the first fully electric D-segment flagship sedan in its Dynasty lineup.

Just 19 days after its launch, BYD said Great Han EV sales reached 4,000 units. At that rate, sales could reach 10,000 or more in its first full month.

With “class-beating high value,” BYD said, “it has firmly established itself in the mid-to-high-end sedan segment above 250,000 yuan,” which is about $37,500.

The Great Han is available in three variants, priced from 235,900 yuan, or about $35,000. Buyers can choose from single- or dual-motor powertrains. The standard rear-wheel-drive (RWD) Premium trim offers up to 1,008 km (626 miles) of CLTC range, while the all-wheel-drive (AWD) Flagship variant offers up to 880 km (546 miles).

All models use a 102.326 kWh BYD Blade 2.0 battery pack. The RWD models have a single 370 kW (496 hp) motor, while the AWD variant adds a 200 kW (268 hp) front motor for a combined 570 kW (764 hp).

Like most of its new vehicles, the Great Han has a roof-mounted LiDAR and BYD’s God’s Eye B, a more advanced version of its intelligent driving system.

The ADAS system offers safety and convenience features, including Navigate on Autopilot on highways and in cities, plus remote autonomous parking.

All variants also include premium features, such as BYD’s DiSus-A dual-chamber air suspension system, rear-wheel steering, and zero-gravity front seats.

Measuring 5,256 mm in length, 1,999 mm in width, and 1,510 mm in height, with a 3,130 mm wheelbase, the Great Han is slightly bigger than the Tesla Model S and Lucid Air. It’s closer in size to the long-wheelbase Mercedes-Benz S-Class.

Thanks to BYD’s second-gen Blade Batteries and Flash Charging technology, the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 70% in just 5 minutes. A full recharge (10% to 97%) takes just 9 minutes.

The Great Han joins the Great Tang SUV as the flagship sedan under BYD’s Dynasty lineup. BYD announced that Great Tang sales reached 14,000 units in October, marking four months of sales above 10,000.

#4449. The Car That Fell to Earth: We Test the 1979 Datsun 310-GX

This little Datsun is still getting in touch with reality.

From the May 1979 issue of Car and Driver.

Datsun is not giving up its small-car territory without a fight. All the adver­tising miles on the new 310 are proof of that. For months now, you’ve seen Dat­sun’s new small car zipping across your TV screen, splashed lavishly over maga­zine pages, and blown up bigger than life on roadside billboards. If Datsun is driven to do anything, it’s to sell 310s.

This ad blitz is understandable, be­cause the 310 is Datsun’s new-genera­tion front-wheel-drive car, a key weapon it will use to defend itself in the world­wide small-car war that’s escalating vi­ciously even now. Moreover, it repre­sents Datsun’s second attempt at build­ing a front-drive sedan, since it’s the successor to the ill-fated F-10. As an ac­knowledged small-car giant, Datsun has a reputation to protect.

To these ends, Datsun has armed itself with a pair of all-new three-door se­dans. They’re named simply the 310 se­dan and the 310-GX—which is the sub­ject of this test. A four-door sedan may be sent over later, but for now, just these two constitute the 310 arsenal. The sedan is the family hauler, while the GX is intended to add a dose of sport to the basic 310 theme. For all practical purposes, the two cars are mechanically identical.

See all results for used cars for sale near 11224

The 310 shares its basic layout with the original F-10. It once again has a 1397 cc four-cylinder engine mounted transversely in the chassis and driving the front wheels. Each corner of the unit body is again suspended independently, with MacPherson struts, coil springs, and an anti-sway bar up front, and trail­ing arms and coil springs in the rear. But aside from these superficial similarities to the old F-10, the new 310 is, as they say, new from bumper to bumper.

Which is just fine by us, because the old F-10 just wasn’t suited to life here on spaceship earth. It was, you’ll re­member, an unearthly amalgam of fun­ny shapes and openings, a cramped and noisy little car that always acted a bit tipsy. In fact, given the way the packaging advantages of front-wheel drive were ignored in the F-10, it could well have been designed three thousand miles in outer space instead of that same distance across the Pacific. About the only things you could say in its favor were that its engine, proven in the B-210, was reliable and that it was good in the snow. Not exactly a rave review.

Datsun wants us to forget the past. It's made every attempt to mold the 310 into a car completely different from its predecessor. And if appearances are anything to go by, it’s accomplished that goal. The old banana-with-windows styling has given way to a fresh-cut wedge profile. And while Datsun hasn’t made the 310 any lower, it has made it longer and noticeably wider. For the record, it’s five inches longer and four inches wider, but—at 2600 pounds­—only 80 pounds heavier. Inside, the handsome velour seats, thick carpeting, and color-keyed dash bespeak a new­found awareness of American tastes. And, standard procedure for Japanese carmakers, Datsun has loaded the 310 chock-full of features designed to make life behind the wheel more pleasant.

See all results for used cars for sale near 11224

Every 310, GX or sedan, comes with reclining seats, a split-back folding rear seat, a slider mechanism that moves the passenger’s bucket forward to facilitate rear-seat entry, a quartz clock, a remote hatch opener, side-window defroster vents, intermittent wipers, power brakes, a remote fuel-filler-door open­er, a rear defogger, and a day-night mir­ror. The sedan also features console-­mounted remote cable controls for the flip-out rear windows. The GX adds roll-down rear quarter-windows, a rear window wiper-washer, a tach, a five­-speed transmission, a four-spoke steer­ing wheel, and fatter, 165/70-13 tires. It certainly seems as though Datsun has wedged the 310 right into the heart of small-car country. Yet despite such favorable first impressions, we found—af­ter living with a GX for more than 2000 miles—that all is still not well with Dat­sun’s front-drive car.

The small-car facts of life have been readily defined for Datsun by such front-line front-drivers as the Rabbit, the Strada, the Omni/Horizon, the Fies­ta, the Civic, and now GM’s formidable new X-body compacts. But when you compare it with its competition, the 310 comes off as little more than an F-10 that fell to earth and isn’t quite in touch with reality yet.

The 310’s interior is a perfect exam­ple of the confusing inconsistencies that compromise the car throughout. Datsun obviously went to a lot of trouble to make the 310’s cabin more hospitable than the F-10’s, yet the effect of the handsome carpeting, dash, and uphol­stery is offset by door panels that look plain enough to have come out of a Dat­sun pickup. Datsun also widened the car to achieve more interior width. This al­leviates the phone-booth claustropho­bia of the F-10—but only for front-seat passengers; rear-seat riders are almost as cramped as they were in the older car. In both new cars, rear legroom is still in severely short supply. Other front-drive cars with the same wheel­base do much better in this respect.

Where the GX really falls down on the job is in the all-important area of day-to-day livability. The 310 is so rid­dled with annoying quirks that its posi­tive qualities are overshadowed.

Take the radio, for instance. Please. Our test car had the optional AM/FM unit. Besides impoverished reception, it was endowed with what has to be one of this decade’s worst speakers—mounted under the dash, facing the floor. Most of the music we could tune in became bad­ly garbled when the volume was turned up loud enough to be heard during highway cruising. You don’t have to lis­ten to the radio, of course, but you’ll find the heating system harder to avoid. When you do use it, you’ll find it only marginally effective. Worse yet, the de­froster—which has to work overtime to get the job done—is about as quiet as an idling 747.

And if you want a little whine before dinner, the 310’s trans­mission will be more than happy to oblige—in any gear. Though the 310’s shift linkage is much improved over the F-10’s Silly Putty unit, the transmission crunched almost every time we grabbed third gear. Then there’s the matter of the shift pattern, which has first down and to the left, off of the H, and re­verse—with no protective lockout­—dead ahead, where any self-respecting low gear ought to be. And sure enough, there is the occasional gnashing of re­verse when making the one-two shift.

Then again, we didn’t like reverse much anyway, because selecting it brought on the annoying warning beeper that is Datsun’s fix for the shift-pattern prob­lem. (It’s there to prevent the unwary from backing away from stoplights when they put the shifter where first is in most other cars.) Last but not least was the vibration problem. At idle, the GX’s engine was so rough that the steering wheel actually got a little blurry around the edges. Nudging the idle up about 100 rpm would solve that prob­lem, but only the engineers will be able to quiet the sharp buzzing of the ex­haust system as the revs climb past 5000—a sound that is the essence of tin­niness. Most of these problems also cropped up on a 310 sedan we were sampling, so they seem to be basic de­sign flaws, not isolated failings of the GX test car.

All of this, when added to the below­ average space utilization, makes the 310 rough-edged—even crude—given the current level of small-car sophistication. That’s unfortunate, because it’s due cause for avoiding what is essentially a fun car to drive. The little engine revs up willingly, and the five-speed—top gear is a direct 1:1 ratio—helps you make good use of the available power. The steering response is direct, and there’s plenty of road feel. Once you get used to the suspension’s initial rubberi­ness when you first twist the wheel, the GX turns out to be a fine fling-around car. It’s also quite stable during highway cruising, and it rides acceptably as well. And of course it’s stingy with your gas money, returning 27 miles for every EPA gallon.

But decent road manners are only part of what makes a good small car. The 310 represents a Datsun move in the right direction, but little more; that it’s superior to the F-10 is frankly not one of the world’s outstanding accom­plishments. This is underscored by the fact that $5500 will probably also buy a well-equipped GM X-body compact. And the 310 can’t begin to match the X­ car’s room, ride, quietness, appoint­ments, and overall refinement—yet its economy is only marginally better. The 310 isn’t in the same league.

So at this point the best news we have is that Datsun’s front-drive car has final­ly come down to earth. But if it’s to live here happily, Datsun will have to try still harder—a lot harder.

Since the subject of this test is the 310 sport coupe, I’ll have to add my vote to the negative side. And that’s too bad, be­cause condemning the sport coupe can, by extension, condemn the sedan that came, afterthought-like, with the deal. My strongest negatives about the sport coupe are its looks (really ugly) and its transmission (really terrible). I don’t have either of those complaints about the sedan. In fact, I think Datsun’s marketeers are in for a surprise. Despite their studied predictions, my hunch is the sporty version will be shunned in the showroom (”Yes, Harry. It’s true. It’s the dreaded Show­room Shun”), and the boxy but cute, sim­ple but contemporary sedan will find favor. And that’s the way it should be, be­cause the 310 sedan is—in the Datsun tradition—a functional, sensible, straightfor­ward transportation module, and that’s what a lot of people are looking for these days. They don’t want an overstyled, beeping aggravation. —Mike Knepper

The Datsun 310, like the Subaru, makes us wonder if there is not a streak of automotive perversity loose among America’s car buyers, and if Datsun may not be on to something big. The 310 simply does not address itself to creature comfort in the way that a Toyota or a Honda does. It is a rather Spartan car, with lots of engine and transmission noise, and very little iso­lation from the mechanical realities. There’s an old-fashioned rough-and­-readiness about the 310 that’s not masked by velour upholstery or cut-pile carpets­—a sort of naïve innocence that appealed to me, along with my belief that it would probably run forever—but I couldn’t ex­plain my affectionate regard for these attributes to my co-testers. Noisy little cars that bucket along as the Datsun does are fun. They bring out an adolescent streak in me that 30 years of automotive experi­ence has been insufficient to suppress. They are amusingly likable in their imper­fections—the four-speed sedan more so than the more pretentious coupe. The 310 didn’t try to kid me, nor did it ever let me down. Only when I learned how much I’d have to pay for those simple, earthy pleasures did my enthusiasm start to flag. —David E. Davis Jr.

General Motors is boosting the long-haul capability of its upcoming half-ton trucks. When the redesigned 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 and GMC Sierra 1500 arrive, models equipped with the popular 3.0-liter Duramax diesel will feature a significantly larger Diesel Exhaust Fluid (DEF) tank. This upgrade marks a major shift for the upcoming truck platform as GM pushes to improve towing efficiency and cross-country range.

The larger DEF tank pairs directly with the new 34-gallon extended-range fuel tanks arriving across the half-ton lineup. For drivers who rely on the Duramax for heavy towing, this means stretching the distance between mandatory fill-ups and minimizing service visits for routine maintenance. This diesel upgrade arrives alongside sweeping changes to the broader engine lineup, which will also introduce larger displacement options and heftier price tags for traditional gasoline buyers.

According to a recent report from GM Authority, GM fitting these larger fluid reservoirs forces a tough design trade-off. To squeeze both the bigger DEF and the massive 34-gallon fuel tank beneath the floorboards, engineers had to completely eliminate the rear under-seat storage bins. For years, owners have relied on these hidden compartments to securely stash expensive tools, emergency gear, and everyday items.

Losing this built-in utility confirms earlier reports that the redesigned trucks would suffer from shrinking cabin volume compared to the outgoing 2026 models. Moving forward, 2027 Silverado and Sierra owners will need to adapt. Drivers will have to depend on the redesigned front center console, stick to the standard gloveboxes, or purchase lockable aftermarket bed boxes to keep their valuables out of sight.

GM is making the right call for its core truck buyers. Customers who spend extra money on the 3.0-liter Duramax diesel care more about uninterrupted highway range and towing convenience than saving a few cubic inches of cab storage. The ability to pull heavy trailers for much longer distances without frantically hunting down a truck stop DEF pump is a massive win for both fleet operators and private owners.

While giving up the rear under-seat storage is definitely frustrating for everyday family utility, the extra fluid capacity ultimately makes the Silverado and Sierra much better workhorses. When weighed against the massive towing and range improvements arriving for the next production cycle, losing a couple of plastic storage bins is a perfectly acceptable trade-off for serious truck owners.

#4447. Scientists discover that cranberry juice may help fight tooth decay

Cranberry juice may offer an unexpected benefit for your teeth. New research suggests that pure, unsweetened cranberry juice can slow the growth of dental plaque and reduce the production of acids that contribute to tooth decay.

Cranberries are a familiar part of holiday celebrations. They appear in sauces, salads, and cocktails, and even serve as colorful seasonal decorations. But beyond their tart flavor and festive appeal, these small red berries contain natural compounds that may support oral health.

Christine Wu, a researcher at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, has been investigating whether cranberry juice could help protect teeth from harmful bacteria. Her findings suggest that the popular beverage may have benefits that go beyond its traditional association with urinary tract health.

How Cranberry Juice Affects Harmful Bacteria

Cranberry juice has long been used to help prevent urinary tract infections. One reason is that cranberries contain compounds called proanthocyanidins, which have anti-inflammatory properties and can interfere with the ability of certain bacteria, including E. coli, to attach to cells.

Wu wanted to determine whether these same compounds might also affect bacteria found in dental plaque. These microorganisms feed on sugars from food and drinks, producing acids that gradually weaken tooth enamel and contribute to cavities.

Rather than testing isolated cranberry compounds, Wu chose to investigate pure cranberry juice, a product people can readily purchase and consume.

"Just like sugar damage is linked to diet, I'm interested in how the food and beverages we consume can help combat the harmful bacteria and benefit our oral health," Wu said.

To investigate the potential effects, researchers conducted a small human study involving 22 participants, including 14 children and eight adults.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three beverages: pure, unsweetened 100% cranberry juice, a cranberry juice cocktail containing 27% juice and added sugar, or plain water.

"It was important to us to conduct these tests with human participants and use products available on the market. Most cranberry juice studies have been conducted using laboratory-prepared cranberry juice extract. Moreover, limited studies have been performed in children," said Wu, who is a professor of pediatric dentistry.

On the morning of the experiment, participants arrived with dental plaque that had accumulated overnight. Researchers first collected plaque samples using cotton swabs on one side of each participant's mouth.

After rinsing with water, participants consumed three small amounts of their assigned beverage. They swished each drink around their mouths several times before swallowing.

Thirty minutes later, researchers collected another set of plaque samples, this time from teeth that had not been swabbed earlier. Comparing the samples allowed the team to examine how each beverage affected plaque activity over the short testing period.

A Surprising Effect on Plaque and Tooth Decay

The results revealed a promising effect of pure cranberry juice. Dental plaque exposed to the unsweetened beverage showed slower regrowth than unexposed plaque samples.

Researchers also found that swishing with pure cranberry juice reduced acid production in dental plaque from both children and adults. This is particularly important because acids produced by oral bacteria can gradually erode tooth enamel, increasing the risk of cavities.

The findings suggest that cranberry juice may interfere with two important processes involved in tooth decay: the buildup of bacterial plaque and the production of damaging acids.

Wu believes these results could eventually support the development of cranberry juice as a "functional beverage" that offers benefits for oral health. The findings are especially interesting because other commonly consumed fruit juices, including orange and apple juice, have not shown the same promise in this research context.

"Most people think of cranberry juice as very sour, very acidic and sugary, and therefore may not contribute positively to oral health. This study found the opposite: that cranberry juice affected dental plaque regrowth and acid production, which may counteract some of the damage done by sugar," she said.

Could Cranberry Juice Become Part of Oral Care?

Although the findings are encouraging, the researchers emphasize that further investigation is necessary. With only 22 participants and a testing period lasting just 30 minutes after consumption, the study cannot establish whether drinking cranberry juice regularly prevents cavities or produces lasting improvements in dental health.

Larger studies conducted over longer periods will be needed to determine whether the observed changes in dental plaque translate into meaningful protection against tooth decay.

Still, Wu sees potential in occasionally using pure cranberry juice as a mouth rinse. One challenge is its intensely tart flavor, which some people may find unpleasant without added sweetness.

"But maybe by adding an appropriate sugar substitute," she said, "to make it a bit more palatable."

The research was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

The Ford Ranger Raptor is the horsepower king among gas-powered midsize pickups, at least on paper, with its 3.0-liter twin-turbocharged EcoBoost V6 producing 405 horsepower. That exceeds the 326-hp output of the 2.4-liter i-Force Max turbo hybrid powertrain in the Toyota Tacoma, America’s best-selling midsize pickup. The Nissan Frontier takes a different approach with its naturally aspirated 3.8-liter V6, but the automaker is apparently exploring a more powerful formula.

At this year’s SEMA Show, Nissan has brought a new Frontier-based concept called the Ronin, which adopts twin-turbocharging hardware from one of the brand’s most iconic nameplates, the GT-R. Both may have the same displacement, but the truck retains its VQ38DD engine rather than swapping in the GT-R’s VR38DETT V6. The automaker didn’t say how much the forced induction boosted its output, but for reference, the regular model already makes 310 horsepower.

This concept is particularly noteworthy given that the production Frontier makes 310 horsepower across the lineup, including the off-road-focused Pro-4X. Some may argue that this is more than enough, even for off-road driving, while others may see the single-engine lineup as limiting its appeal, especially compared with the Ford Ranger, which offers multiple engine options.

Nissan paired the GT-R-derived turbocharging system with EcuTek engine management, a custom front-mounted intercooler, dual off-road air intakes, and a Nismo Off Road exhaust. The suspension also received extensive upgrades, including modified Titan components, a rear axle swap, Bilstein Black Hawk shocks, and custom racing control arms. CJD Racing’s long-travel suspension components provide a four-inch lift, a 12-inch wider track, and 14 inches of suspension travel.

Other notable modifications include a custom front fascia, grille, and bumpers; prototype Nismo Off Road fender flares and running lights; Nismo Off Road 6-inch driving lights, 4-inch A-pillar lights, rock sliders, and all-weather floor mats; custom Kinetic sport bucket seats; and a dashboard gauge pod displaying boost, oil pressure, and exhaust temperature.

As a concept truck, the Frontier Ronin has no confirmed production plans, though Nissan can gather feedback that could influence future products. The automaker cites the Rock Creek lineup as an example of how previous SEMA concepts have inspired production models. So, with enough interest, the Japanese marque might consider adding a new, more powerful trim above the Pro-4X, potentially matching or even exceeding the Ranger Raptor’s horsepower on paper.

Nissan has already collaborated with Roush Performance to build a more extreme version of the Frontier called the Pro-4X R, featuring upgrades such as a two-inch suspension lift, Öhlins 2.0 off-road shocks, and 17-inch titanium-finished wheels. However, it retains the standard powertrain.

Aside from the Frontier Ronin, the automaker has brought two other concepts to the 2026 SEMA Show: the Pathfinder XE-V6 Concept, which celebrates the model’s 40th anniversary, and the Armada Jungle Patrol Concept. The event runs from November 3 to 6 at the Las Vegas Convention Center.

#4444. 1985 Ford F-250 Restomod Sends Raptor Brand to the ’80s at SEMA

Matt Johnson’s 1985 F-250 Raptor-inspired build was backed by Ford Performance and will be part of Ford’s display at SEMA this year.

Ford’s first Raptor didn’t arrive until 2008 at the 41st Baja 1000 in Ensenada, Mexico. The high-performance F-150 SVT Raptor-R had a podium finish, and the Raptor name continues to grace the widened bodywork of some of Ford’s most powerful pickups.

But imagine if Raptor had come around about two decades earlier. It might’ve looked like Matt Johnson’s Raptor-inspired 1985 F-250, which is getting a huge reveal at Ford’s SEMA booth this year.

The F-250 project actually started with an old Toyota Land Cruiser, which Johnson had planned to put an EcoBoost engine into. A call to Ford Racing Parts led to discussions about a collaboration between the automaker and Johnson, who restores older off-roading vehicles and documents the process on social media.

See all results for new 2027 Ford Super Duty for sale near 52218

A few months later, Ford suggested putting a small-block Heritage motor in the Land Cruiser. Johnson bounced back with a photo of a 1985 F-250 with a blown engine that had been sitting behind his shop. He felt the small-block was better suited for a classic Ford, and the bullnose F-250 seemed like a perfect candidate.

Soon, Johnson’s $800 shop truck, called Norma Jeane, was getting a full makeover backed by Ford Performance. The truck’s original engine was replaced with Ford Racing’s 575-hp 460-cubic-inch Boss V-8. He paired the small-block with a Ford R680 six-speed automatic transmission.

Johnson documented the transformation through a 92-part series on social media. His daily updates covered everything, from installing a custom-made suspension kit to weatherstripping the windows. Though a lot of the truck is now brand new, the F-250 maintains its distinctly ‘80s qualities, right down to the hubcaps and vintage-style stereo.

The build was originally meant to be completed in 40 days, but when Ford proposed the idea of bringing it to SEMA, that 40-day timeline shifted to a much longer saga. Along the way, Johnson has accumulated 425,000 followers on Instagram and even more on Facebook under his Doc Johnson Restorations shop account. His latest post shows the F-250 getting loaded into a transport truck and beginning the journey from his small shop in Klamath Falls, Oregon, to SEMA in Las Vegas.

“Honestly, it’s a crazy story, and I feel blessed to be a part of it,” Johnson said in a press release. “The truck—and the project itself—took on a life of its own. In many ways, I’m just along for the ride.” Johnson and his Raptor-inspired F-250 will be a part of Ford’s display at SEMA, which takes place November 3-6 in Las Vegas, Nevada.

Even some of the most popular, highly regarded cars in the world have their quirks. We found out that much with the latest Toyota RAV4, which has a center console design that many owners have found compromises comfort. It turns out that the Honda CR-V, the RAV4’s fiercest rival, has an unusual pain point of its own. The best-selling SUV in the U.S. this year so far, numerous CR-V owners have uncovered flaws in the Honda’s windshield wiper design. One would imagine that getting a wiper design wrong in 2026 is near impossible, but a lot of CR-V owners have been left frustrated by the wiper system’s inability to properly clean the windshield.

There are two separate issues with the CR-V’s wiper design, both of which have been spoken about at length on several social media forums. We also found complaints listed on the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) website.

The first issue involves the placement of the wiper system spray nozzles, which are situated on the wiper arms themselves. Many owners have found that when attempting to clean the windshield, the nozzles only begin spraying water when the wiper blades are roughly halfway up the windshield. As a result, many owners have complained that it’s not possible to properly clean the windshield, particularly in snowy or icy conditions, where hood-mounted nozzles would be more practical and better able to disperse the water.

“I will die on this hill. The wipers (especially when I’m using them w/windshield wiper fluid) are my ONLY gripe about this car. The design is terrible,” said one owner on Reddit.

“Having the windshield wiper fluid come out of the blades rather than spraying directly onto the windshield is useless as the fluid comes out while the wipers are half way up and fluid then gets pushed off the windshield and flows down the driver’s side window again affecting the driver’s visibility,” said another owner of a 2023 CR-V, who is based in Connecticut. This owner shared their experience on the NHTSA’s website.

These wiper-mounted nozzles are meant to eliminate the wind deflection or blind spots created by traditional, hood-mounted nozzles, but it appears that the current CR-V’s nozzles have not been properly engineered.

The second issue involves the driver’s-side wiper, which several owners say does not reach the edge of the windshield on the left. This leaves a significant portion of the windshield covered in dirt, creating another visibility concern. Some owners say the wipers only work properly if the vehicle is in Accessory Mode, while others were told by dealerships that the gap left on the driver’s side is normal.

“While driving my 2025 Hybrid CRV with 4K miles in a light rain, the wiper stopped going all the way to the edge and now only goes 90% of the way up no matter the setting. In a heavy rain, it will go 96%, and in accessory mode it goes up 100% of the way,” said an owner of a 2025 CR-V on Reddit. Other owners in the thread reported the same issue, with many filing complaints with the NHTSA and hoping for a recall. After all, visibility-related safety defects are often considered serious enough to initiate a recall.

A video posted by another Reddit user shows that an unacceptably large portion of the CR-V’s windshield isn’t reached by the left wiper blade, with a few commenters suggesting that it’s a software issue, not a mechanical alignment problem.

How to change wiper blades and washer fluid | Autoblog Wrenched

Manufacturers have invested heavily in technologies that enhance driver visibility, from blind-spot monitoring systems to surround-view monitors and pedestrian detection systems. But all of that doesn’t mean much if one of the most basic safety features, the windshield wiper, doesn’t do its job properly. At the very least, the performance of the current CR-V’s windshield wipers are inconsistent from one model to the next. While no recall has been issued for this condition and windshield wiper testing does not form part of safety tests run by the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, that does not mean there isn’t a genuine concern. As visibility impacts overall safety, we would like to see Honda address the concern.

#4442. Why some “lower-risk” childhood cancers turn deadly

Some childhood cancers may be far more dangerous than their initial risk classification suggests. Scientists have discovered that certain tumors considered less threatening can contain hidden populations of highly aggressive cancer cells, potentially explaining why some children experience devastating outcomes despite lacking the usual genetic warning signs.

The discovery could change how doctors identify children at risk of life-threatening cancer, allowing treatment to be better matched to the true aggressiveness of their disease.

The findings, published in Cancer Research, come from scientists at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, the University of Cambridge, Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), University College London, and collaborating institutions. Their research focused on rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS), an aggressive cancer that develops from muscle tissue and is among the most common soft tissue cancers affecting children younger than 15. Approximately 55 children are diagnosed with the disease in the United Kingdom each year.[1]

Unlike many adult cancers, which can develop after years of aging or exposure to environmental factors, childhood cancers often result from genetic changes that occur during early development.

Why Some Childhood Cancers Defy Risk Predictions

Doctors generally divide rhabdomyosarcoma into two main categories based on whether a tumor carries a particular genetic warning sign. This marker occurs when two genes that are normally separate become fused together, creating an abnormal genetic combination associated with especially aggressive disease.[2]

Children whose tumors contain this fusion have substantially lower survival rates than those without it, even when they receive intensive treatment.

But this classification has a troubling limitation. Some children whose tumors lack the high-risk genetic marker still develop aggressive cancers that can prove fatal. Until now, scientists have struggled to explain why these supposedly less dangerous tumors sometimes behave so aggressively.

To investigate this mystery, the research team compared tumors from children with different forms of rhabdomyosarcoma, looking beyond the genetic markers traditionally used to estimate risk.

The researchers examined tumor samples from 16 children, including four whose cancers lacked the fusion marker but proved fatal, four with fusion-positive tumors, and eight children with fusion-negative disease who remained alive.

Using advanced genetic analysis, scientists studied the tumors at a level of detail that conventional techniques cannot easily achieve.

One of their main tools was single-cell RNA sequencing, a technology that measures gene activity in individual cells. Rather than examining a tumor as a single mass, this approach allows researchers to investigate the behavior of its different cell populations and identify potentially dangerous cells that might otherwise go unnoticed.

The scientists also used spatial transcriptomics, a technique that maps gene activity to specific locations within a tumor. This provided a clearer picture of where aggressive cancer cells were concentrated and how they were distributed throughout the tissue.

The results revealed a striking similarity between tumors that had previously been placed in different risk categories. Some cancers classified as non-high-risk contained cells with gene activity patterns closely resembling those found in high-risk tumors.

Even more surprisingly, these aggressive tumors did not need the same genetic mutations to produce similar behavior. Researchers identified rare genetic changes that affected many of the same cellular pathways involved in the most dangerous forms of the disease.

This suggests that different genetic abnormalities can ultimately push cancer cells toward a shared aggressive state. In other words, tumors can reach a similarly dangerous biological condition through multiple genetic routes, even when they lack the warning sign typically used to identify high-risk disease.

Dr. Karin Straathof, co-senior author at UCL Cancer Institute and GOSH, said:

"By studying tumors one cell at a time, we uncovered hidden populations of aggressive cancer cells that conventional methods miss. Although these tumors carry different genetic changes, many converge on the same aggressive pathways. This helps explain why some children who appear to have lower-risk disease can still have a devastating outcome."

A New Path Toward More Precise Cancer Treatment

The findings could have important implications for how childhood cancer is diagnosed and treated.

If doctors can identify the distinctive biological signatures of aggressive cancer cells at diagnosis, they may be able to recognize children who face a greater risk of relapse or death, even when standard genetic tests suggest otherwise.

Such an approach could also help prevent unnecessary treatment. Children with genuinely lower-risk tumors might avoid some of the harmful side effects associated with intensive chemotherapy, while those with hidden aggressive disease could receive stronger or more targeted treatment earlier.

The researchers are particularly interested in identifying markers that could be used to develop therapies aimed specifically at the most dangerous cancer cells.

One possible direction involves immunotherapy, including CAR-T cell therapy. This treatment uses specially modified immune cells to recognize and attack cancer cells. Although such treatments would require further development and testing for rhabdomyosarcoma, they could eventually offer a more precise alternative to conventional chemotherapy, potentially reducing damage to healthy tissues.

Scientists are now expanding their research to include hundreds of additional tumor samples. By studying a much larger group of patients, they hope to uncover more of the rare genetic changes capable of producing aggressive cancer and accelerate the development of personalized treatments.

Sara Wakeling, Chief Executive Officer and co-founder of Alice's Arc, said:

"Every child with cancer deserves the best possible chance of survival. We're proud to support research into rhabdomyosarcoma, showing how cutting-edge technologies can uncover the biology driving aggressive childhood cancers. These discoveries bring us closer to more personalized treatments and better outcomes for children."

Dr. Laura Danielson, Children's and Young Person's Lead at Cancer Research UK, said:

"Discovery research like this is essential to understand the unique biology of these cancers. This important study demonstrates that aggressive tumors may share similar features, even if they carry different genetic changes. By helping researchers understand what these high-risk cancers have in common, this work adds a vital piece to the puzzle and could help guide future efforts to improve treatment for children and young people with rhabdomyosarcoma."

Rethinking How Doctors Identify Dangerous Childhood Cancers

Beyond its potential treatment applications, the discovery challenges a fundamental assumption about how rhabdomyosarcoma should be classified.

Instead of viewing aggressive disease primarily through the presence or absence of one genetic abnormality, the researchers suggest that doctors may need to consider the broader biological state of the cancer cells themselves.

This distinction is important because tumors with different mutations can behave in remarkably similar ways. Identifying the shared features of aggressive disease could provide a more reliable way to recognize children who need intensive treatment, regardless of the particular genetic changes driving their tumors.

Professor Sam Behjati, co-senior author formerly at the Wellcome Sanger Institute and Head of the Department of Paediatrics at the University of Cambridge, said:

"This work changes how we think about rhabdomyosarcoma. Rather than a single, abnormal gene, we've shown that there is an overarching cell state of aggressive disease that defies conventional classification systems. Understanding this shared biology could help identify children who need more intense treatment to improve their survival."

Although further research is needed before these findings can change routine clinical care, they provide a promising foundation for more accurate risk assessments and treatments tailored to each child's cancer.

By revealing aggressive behavior hidden beneath seemingly reassuring genetic classifications, scientists hope to improve survival for children with the most dangerous tumors while sparing others from treatment they may not need.

The research received support through a Cancer Research UK -- Children with Cancer UK Innovation Award, with additional co-funding from Alice's Arc and funding from Wellcome.

#4441. 8 Switch Metroidvanias That Respect Your Time

Shayna Josi is a Features Writer from South Africa. She is a ghostwriter, copywriter, and editor in the publishing industry.

People are busy and don’t have time to sink hundredss of hours into a game. I love a sprawling game, but every single one boasting a hundred-hour-long campaign is just not feasible. It’s even worse when the game is artificially bloated with bad check points and constant backtracking.

From kitchen sink refills to dinosaur eggs and rabbit's feet, Stardew Valley hides a surprising number of details even devoted fans haven't found yet.

There are a lot of Metroidvanias that take a long time to complete, but not all of them are massive time sinks. There are some Metroidvanias that have either streamlined their mechanics for easier gameplay, or they’re short and sweet. If you're looking for a Switch Metroidvania that respects your time, these ones are well worth considering.

Not every Metroidvania needs to be brutally difficult to be rewarding, and a lot of the time small games punch above their weight class. Islets is one such game —it's a charming adventure with very forgiving combat and random time limited upgrades that affect exploration and your combat capabilities. While you still need to learn attack patterns for boss fights, it’s significantly less difficult than most other Metroidvanias.

Islets also has great level design, which uses an interconnected structure that gives you plenty of reasons to revisit locations you’ve already visited. Doing so isn’t unnecessarily complicated, and having a reason to backtrack makes it feel worthwhile rather than a slog.

Sometimes, the best way to respect the player's time is to deliver a fantastic experience and know when to end it. Gato Roboto is a short Metroidvania that ends on a high note, before it overstays its welcome.

Gato Roboto’s monochromatic presentation gives it a distinctive retro aesthetic, and being able to play as a cat is charming and fun. The environments are relatively compact, which makes sense for a small creature like a cat, but that also makes for straightforward navigation. You'll still discover new abilities and encounter challenging bosses, but the adventure rarely feels like it's padding its runtime with unnecessary bloat.

Record of Lodoss War: Deedlit in Wonder Labyrinth is a relatively short Metroidvania that makes its inspiration from Castlevania games more obvious even than other Metroidvania games. Its environments and progression system make it a good choice if you want a focused adventure.

There are a lot of video games out there that instill a sense of discovery in its players, but not every single one can be called a Metroidvania.

Record of Lodoss War: Deedlit in Wonder Labyrinth is short and sweet: it can be completed in approximately five to six hours, depending on how much time you spend exploring. Its story is straightforward, which means it's perfect if you want to turn your brain off and focus on combat. Because it's so short, it's perfect for a weekend or a night in.

Touhou Luna Nights takes a particularly interesting approach to Metroidvania combat because it introduces time manipulation as one of its central mechanics. As you progress through the levels, you'll encounter increasingly challenging enemies and bosses that require you to understand how your time-manipulation abilities work.

The mechanic is particularly effective because it influences almost every aspect of the experience, a sign of good game design and makes sure that every mechanic does something productive. Touhou Luna Nights is also relatively short, taking approximately five hours to complete. The intentional design means you can enjoy it without having to spend dozens of hours working through repetitive encounters.

If you're looking for a Metroidvania that prioritizes combat and movement, Blade Chimera is worth checking out. Blade Chimera combines the traditional Metroidvania level design with a unique weapon mechanic that changes up combat and makes it more interesting.

Because of its focus on the weapon mechanic, there's also considerable emphasis on responsive combat and movement. Its progression system gives you opportunities to improve your character's capabilities without making repetitive grinding the central focus of the experience. This is the perfect game if you like Metroidvania combat without the frustration you get in Soulslikes. The warp skill makes travel instantaneous, and removes a lot of needless repetition.

Astalon: Tears of the Earth is one of the more traditional Metroidvanias on this list. It shows that good level design can make longer games feel short, and it does that by centering its exploration around a tower. Because you can freely switch between three characters with different abilities, there's some strategy required to excel in this game.

If you're looking for unexplored gems in video games, I recommend these ten Metroidvanias that are unexpected masterpieces.

Astalon is considerably more challenging and demanding than many other Metroidvanias, but its carefully constructed environments make the additional time feel purposeful. It's a great choice if you enjoy that classic Metroidvania design and want something that offers a little more depth.

Ori and the Blind Forest is one of those games that changes you. It's a whimsical, beautiful, and emotional experience, and yet it also understands the importance of maintaining momentum, something that's crucial for good game design. Because of this, its exploration feels like an important part of the journey, rather than something you have to endure between major encounters.

Ori avoids tedious backtracking with a Soul Link checkpoint system, which lets you place your own checkpoints. This gives you considerably more control over your progress and allows you to prepare for particularly challenging sections. It's just one mechanic that forms the greater whole of a good game.

Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown is arguably one of the best examples of a modern Metroidvania that respects the player's time. While its interconnected world is packed with things to do, it also includes several quality-of-life mechanics that make exploration considerably less frustrating.

One of these mechanics is the Memory Shard system, which allows you to simply refer back to your screenshots when you've acquired the necessary abilities. Guided Mode is also a big help, as it shows you where to go next without forcing you to follow a predetermined route. These mechanics guide you rather than hold your hand, but they're a lifesaver that stops you from getting stuck in one place for hours and reaching for a guide.

#4440. 2027 Harley-Davidson Sprint 440 Harkens Back to a Simpler Time

Harley-Davidson’s new entry-level motorcycle resurrects a classic name and its single-cylinder formula.

Given the price of, well, everything these days, affordability and accessibility are unsurprisingly hot buzzwords in the motorcycle industry. And brands that’ve embraced them are reaping the benefits. Bikes like Triumph’s 400 range and Royal Enfield’s 350 range—lightweight, inexpensive, modest-capacity single-cylinder—are practically flying off showroom floors. Up until now, that’s described nothing in Harley-Davidson’s stable, at least for US riders. But that changes with the 2027 Harley-Davidson Sprint 440.

See all results for used cars for sale near 83440

While the Bar and Shield basically bleeds V-twins, the brand hasn’t only made two-cylinder bikes. Its earliest models, often called “Silent Gray Fellows,” had single-cylinder engines. And if the new Sprint 440’s name seems familiar to you, it’s because Harley sold single-powered bikes with that nameplate in the 1960s and 1970s.

While those Sprints were built in Italy, the US-market Sprint 440s will be built in Harley’s York, Pennsylvania factory. Admittedly, this new Sprint technically derives from the single-cylinder Harley that’s already been on sale elsewhere for several years: the X440 developed together with the Indian company Hero MotoCorp. But still, don’t cry heresy, Milwaukee faithful.

It might use a vintage name and manufacturing formula, but the 2027 Sprint 440 is a thoroughly modern Harley-Davidson. Its 440cc two-valve air/oil-cooled single-cylinder engine—fuel-injected, unlike the carbureted original Sprints—makes 27 hp and 28 pound-feet, sent to the rear wheel via a slip-assist clutch and six-speed transmission. That rear wheel is 17 inches in diameter, with the front being 19 inches; both are cast aluminum. And when the Sprint needs to stop, er, sprinting, you’ve got ABS-equipped disc brakes.

If that doesn’t seem like enough scream for this eagle, know that the Royal Enfield Meteor 350 cruiser’s 394cc single-cylinder engine makes 20 hp and 20 pound-feet. Also, according to the spec sheets, the Sprint 440 is slightly lighter: a claimed 412 pounds to the Meteor 350’s 421 pounds. The Sprint is that much lighter than the upcoming Triumph Bonneville T40 as well, though the Triumph’s 398cc liquid-cooled single makes 30 hp (and other Triumph 400 models make around 40 hp). But, in another accessibility nod, the Meteor 350’s and Bonneville T4’s seats are 30.1 and 32.2 inches high, respectively, while Harley claims a 26.4-inch laden seat height for the Sprint. All three of these bikes have preload-adjustable dual rear shocks, though unlike the other two, the Sprint 440’s forks are inverted.

See all results for used cars for sale near 83440

Moving on, the 2027 Harley-Davidson Sprint 440 has a color TFT display (something quickly becoming de rigeur). The 3.5-inch circular gauge shows a speedometer, tachometer, odometer, and trip meter as well as the usual warning lights and turn signals. Those turn signals, like the headlight and taillight, are LED. And there’s one of the other modern motorcycling necessities, a USB-C charging port, above the headlight. Additionally, Harley-Davidson will offer numerous accessories for the Sprint 440, including a windshield, engine guard, saddlebags, and (predictably) skull adornments. Also, if the regular seat isn’t the right height, there will be multiple seat options to dial in your proper fit.

OK, accessibility seems fine, but what about that affordability? When Harley-Davidson first announced it was resurrecting the Sprint, it claimed the bike would cost around $6000. As of this writing, U.S. pricing hasn’t been revealed. However, in Canada, the Sprint 440 will cost $8499 CAD, which is about $6100 at current exchange rates. That’s roughly $1000 more than a 2027 Royal Enfield Meteor 350, though it’s around what Triumph charges for its 400 models.

But, crucially, it’s almost $4000 less expensive than Harley’s current entry-level model, the 975cc Nightster. And while everything’s expensive these days, four grand still buys quite a bit of gasoline for riding. We’ll just have to wait until spring 2027 to see if the Sprint 440 hits the ground running.

After discovering car magazines and Fast and Furious movies in high school, Matthew Skwarczek wanted to create cleaner fuels to keep automobiles around. But after a brief engineering career, the Chicagoland native realized he preferred researching and writing about the cars themselves. That's how he found himself first at MotorBiscuit and then at C/D. Today, when he’s not reading, he’s daydreaming on Bring a Trailer, backpacking, or riding his motorcycle or bicycle.

#4439. Rolls-Royce Says Its Average Customer Is 43, Down from 56

Kia's Telluride Is Closing In On The Sportage's U.S. Sales Crown

Ford Crams The Most Powerful OEM Crate Engine Ever Made Into New Bronco Concept

Mercedes-Benz Wants To Blow Snow Off Your Car Before You Open The Door

Rolls-Royce has apparently lowered the average age of its customers to 43 and has even attracted Gen-Zs to its showrooms.

Kia's Telluride Is Closing In On The Sportage's U.S. Sales Crown

Ford Crams The Most Powerful OEM Crate Engine Ever Made Into New Bronco Concept

Mercedes-Benz Wants To Blow Snow Off Your Car Before You Open The Door

Shaq Spent $1.3 Million on 3 Rolls-Royces to Spite a Salesman

We want you to imagine a Rolls-Royce owner. If you pictured someone a little bit older, then we can’t blame you. The name conjures images of old-world luxury with massive estates and links to royalty. It’s either that or said owner is a captain of industry, being whisked away to important social gatherings across cities.

But while the automaker still offers traditional luxury in spades, it’s also managed to lower the average age of its buyers. As it turns out, classic luxury cars have a strong appeal for younger, affluent shoppers. The thing is, Rolls-Royce didn’t just become a brand that suddenly attracted a new era of customers, but rather, it made the effort to make it happen.

Julian Jenkins is the director of sales and brand for Rolls-Royce, and he recently told Automotive News that the average customer is 43 years old. You read that right; it’s older millennials who are now buying these cars. Before 2010, the average age was 56 years old, so how did the brand do it?

He added that, in some markets, the brand is showing relevance among the ultra-wealthy Gen-Z crowd. “In China, for example, we have some of our youngest clients who are in their mid to late 20s,” said Jenkins. There’s no doubt that China played a part in making Rolls-Royce a ‘young’ brand.

Jenkins pointed out that the Cullinan played a key role in bringing in younger customers to the marque, but it’s not the only reason for the drop in average ages. “Black Badge, Cullinan and also some of our bespoke creations have done that,” Jenkins said, further adding that it’s the ultra-exclusive Coachbuild division models such as the Boat Tail and Droptail actually attracting a younger crowd. “Those are Rolls-Royce models that have stimulated interest,” added the executive.

Rolls-Royce has since responded to the new wave of customers by transforming its showrooms. Case in point, Rolls-Royce Motor Cars Beverly Hills went from merely selling cars to a place that hosts gatherings with its speakeasy-inspired lounge and bar. It’s called the Black Badge Lounge, and before anyone dismisses it as a gimmick, it’s actually become a destination for current and prospective owners. The showroom overhaul gives the client a more immersive experience.

Rival Bentley has also adapted a similar approach when it unveiled its new look for its shops. Jack Barclay Bentley in London was the first to get the boutique treatment, and like Rolls-Royce Beverly Hills, a large part of the store is dedicated as a bar that doubles as the reception area. As for Mercedes, it’s building standalone stores for the Maybach division to provide an exclusive and unique experience that’s far elevated from the usual Mercedes-Benz showroom. The aim is to make the visit feel less transactional and more warm and welcoming.

Also, Milton Pedraza, CEO of Luxury Institute, mentioned that the baby boomers who once made up a big chunk of Rolls-Royce sales are gradually fading out. Instead of simply sticking firmly to tradition, the British automaker managed to infuse its values while tailoring it to a new generation of customers. “Rolls-Royce truly is an iconic brand. It’s one of those like Hermes: It’s been around for generations and it continues to reinvent itself. Now reinventing itself into more bespoke. You pay half a million for the base and then you spend another half a million on ‘Customize it for me,'” said Pedraza.

Of course, the brand’s customers have always wanted a more bespoke vehicle, so it’s not a generational thing. The difference now is, it’s tweaked the formula and moved with the times.
